quarterly_data.signal: CALL — THE FIBER-CONTENT-PER-GPU FRAMEWORK (the definitive supply-side math for optical in AI factories). Base case: enterprise grows at the rate GPUs grow; THREE drivers add on top. (1) CLUSTER SIZE: clusters ABOVE ~130,000 GPUs exceed a 512-radix switch's two-layer span and need a THIRD OPTICAL LAYER -> ~50% MORE CONTENT PER GPU for very large clusters. (2) BANDWIDTH (doubles ~every 2 years): Hopper -> Blackwell kept 100G SerDes so fibers went 8 -> 16 per GPU (content DOUBLED); the RUBIN era jumps SerDes to 200G with lane count flat -> NEUTRAL; Feynman (~2029-30): fibers double again IF SerDes stays 200G, neutral if 400G arrives (BiDi/WDM could offset) — Springboard conservatively assumes NEUTRAL. (3) SCALE-UP, today 100% COPPER: Vera Rubin Ultra NVL576 is a HYBRID step — copper inside each 72-GPU rack, DIRECT OPTICAL rack-to-rack. Bracketing a full-optical scale-up: 14.4 Tbps scale-up / 200G = 72 lanes x 2 fibers = 144, plus scale-out 1.6 Tbps / 200G = 16 fibers -> 160 FIBERS PER GPU = 10x today's 16-fiber scale-out-only content (reality lands between; % of optical ports is confidential). COMBINED: optical content per GPU +1.3-1.5x BY 2028 and 'much, much higher' toward 2030. Status: Q2 enterprise strength is 'ALL JUST SCALE-OUT — we are not yet seeing scale-up or photonics in our results'; orders accelerating; 'if we could make more, we could sell more.'
quarterly_data.figure: Content/GPU drivers: 3rd optical layer >130k GPUs (+50%); Blackwell 16 fibers; full-optical scale-up = 160 fibers/GPU (10x); +1.3-1.5x by 2028

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — PHOTONICS: A $10B MAP BY 2030, AND THE LTA MODEL: Corning's new PHOTONICS Market-Access Platform targets $10 BILLION of revenue by 2030 — passive photonics INSIDE THE BOX (FAU harnesses and everything that moves/manages light between the faceplate and the silicon-photonics optical engine) for CPO/NPO, where Corning historically had ZERO content; likely starts with scale-out, and optical SCALE-UP supercharges it; the plan is built on 'assumptions and discussions AND AGREEMENTS with customers.' Despite industry chatter on scale-up timing, 'NO CHANGES to our fundamental belief... inside the real ecosystem there is much less drama than what it looks like from outside.' Business model: long-term agreements (Amazon multi-billion, NVIDIA, Meta up-to-$6B, Apple) will be 'the LION'S SHARE of our optical business' — every major capacity expansion is underpinned by risk/reward-sharing LTAs; profitability comes from innovation value-share, not bare-fiber pricing (optical NI +77% to a record 21% margin). Springboard math: run rate $20B by end-2026 (Q3 guide may hit it a QUARTER EARLY) -> $30B (2028) -> $40B (2030), 19% CAGR; high-confidence variant $27B/$35B; biggest risk-adjustment between the two = SCALE-UP TIMING. Elsewhere: memory prices push handsets down mid-teens % (Gorilla outperforms on content) but push TVs LARGER/premium (favors Gen 10.5); solar recovers from Q3 toward a $3B stream, with MORE POLYSILICON SHIFTING TO SEMICONDUCTOR (ELECTRONIC) GRADE at Hemlock; FY capex ~$2B.

With the Lumen extension, the Zayo agreement and the new Verizon deal, management now expects to reach that number much sooner than the end of the decade and believes the opportunity is bigger than that, with an update to follow. Corning's dense fiber cables — more fibers in the same cable diameter — are the reason it is winning DCI, and are what it sells Lumen.

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and constraints: Corning is not fiber constrained today but expects to be, which is why it committed to significantly increase US fiber capacity at what it calls the world's largest, lowest-cost fiber factory; that capacity starts coming online in the not that distant future and is tied to customer agreements. Cable and connectivity capacity has been added quarter over quarter for close to a year, and connectivity is where Corning expects to be most constrained relative to today's capacity as scale-up drives growth. Customers are funding part of the build through deposits they earn back by purchasing, and Corning modularises capacity adds rather than bringing on a whole factory at a time.

quarterly_data.signal: Photonics timing sharpened: Corning is planning to build out a $10 billion business by the end of the decade, from no sales today, selling into NPO and CPO applications inside the server tray, and is building out the supply chain now — hopefully next year we will start to see some sales there. The single biggest variable for the Springboard high-confidence gap is CPO adoption; the CPO supply chain at the scale required does not exist today and is the largest build investors should watch, though management sees no showstopper. Schlesinger expects the adoption inflection in the next four or five years rather than in 2027, with near-term content coming from traditional product sets (polarization-maintaining fiber, FAUs) and GlassBridge-type products a 2030-plus opportunity. Scale-up of the network should begin at the end of next year and run 2028 through 2030; today's growth is scale-out, where clusters above 130,000 GPUs add another network layer.

There is a broad effort to bring optics into scale-up, closer to the GPUs and switch ASICs; he believes those links going to photons, with Corning's innovations playing a significant role, is inevitable. Lumentum remains confident in an ultra-high-power laser chip demand ramp in the second half of calendar 2027, ahead of customer scale-up deployments in calendar 2028. Because the first phase of scale-up optical connections spans across compute racks within a cluster, the ramp applies to any topology larger than one rack. Ultra-high-power laser revenue is expected to reach roughly the $50 million mark by the end of calendar 2026, with the first triple-digit ($100M+) quarter expected in fiscal Q3 FY2027.

quarterly_data.signal: NPO (near-packaged optics) called 'completely additive' and 'significantly increasing the optical TAM.' Two laser types are being evaluated for NPO: a mid-power laser integrated directly into the optical engine, and a high-power laser in an external light source module. Lumentum's NPO/CPO laser family spans 120 mW, 150 mW, and 400 mW output levels off common design and process know-how. Wupen Yuen: each NPO set carries ~6.4T of bandwidth, roughly four times a local module, and NPO should hit the market in the late 2027 / 2028 timeframe to enable optical scale-up.

The margin gap between CW and EML 'has closed considerably' since the prior call (EML still better). quarterly_data.signal: Narrow linewidth laser assembly shipments grew sequentially for the 10th consecutive quarter and were up over 130% year-over-year. Scale-across demand is being driven by inferencing and training applications requiring full-rate connectivity between data centers, plus political and regulatory constraints favoring smaller, more modular builds. Scale of the DCI opportunity: for one major hyperscaler, the network capacity connecting just two AI data center sites is double the total global backbone capacity that hyperscaler built over the entirety of the last decade.
quarterly_data.figure: narrow linewidth +130% YoY, 10th consecutive sequential growth quarter

quarterly_data.signal: Cloud transceivers: record 800G shipments in the quarter while initiating production of next-generation 1.6T modules. Transceiver profitability continues to improve on yield gains, capacity utilization, and the initial rollout of higher-ASP 1.6T units. 1.6T uptake is expected to intensify starting in fiscal Q1 FY2027 and sustain through calendar 2027, anchored by lead Tier 1 hyperscale customers rolling out custom AI clusters. Management believes Lumentum is first to market ahead of larger competitors in many instances and can hold that share advantage through the cycle, crediting its signal integrity team on difficult 1.6T designs.
quarterly_data.figure: record 800G shipments; 1.6T production initiated; 1.6T uptake intensifies from fiscal Q1 FY2027

quarterly_data.signal: OCS: shipments doubled from fiscal Q3 to fiscal Q4, and Q1 FY2027 guidance includes Lumentum's first triple-digit OCS revenue quarter - expected to be 'meaningfully above the three-digit mark' ($100M+). Tracking to (not ahead of) the previously stated $400 million of OCS shipments for the second half of calendar 2026, leaving room to run in the fourth calendar quarter. Demand signal for 2027 'continues to be incredibly strong'; initial work started to add capacity with contract manufacturers alongside increasing internal factory output. Lumentum describes itself as the only merchant OCS supplier with a shipping track record, and expects to cross over to become the number one OCS supplier sometime in early 2027 versus one customer's internal source of supply.
quarterly_data.figure: OCS shipments 2x QoQ; first $100M+ OCS quarter guided; $400M H2 CY2026 on track; #1 supplier expected early 2027

quarterly_data.signal: OCS roadmap broadened since the prior call: Lumentum is now planning higher and lower port count products, including specialized in-tray offerings. These are entirely additive to the TAM presented at OFC and are expected to hit in the 2028 timeframe, requiring significant engineering redesign.
quarterly_data.figure: OCS in-tray and higher/lower port-count products; additive TAM; 2028 timeframe

quarterly_data.signal: Greensboro, North Carolina fab (fifth InP fab, acquired March 2026): conversion from gallium arsenide to indium phosphide is 'well underway,' with long-pole items such as reactors already addressed. No change to schedule - first revenue in early 2028, ramping through calendar 2028 to full pitch by end of 2028 and into 2029. Capacity remains uncommitted and Lumentum is actively talking to customers about laser demand, expecting to announce new Greensboro arrangements (LTAs) over the next couple of quarters.
quarterly_data.figure: Greensboro GaAs-to-InP conversion underway; first revenue early 2028; ramp into 2029; LTAs in discussion

quarterly_data.signal: InP substrate supply: after a surge in ultra-high-power laser demand across a couple of customers, Lumentum spent the last three months securing additional substrate supply and signed a deal with AXT during the quarter. Hurlston: 'we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT. They are a great partner.' Lumentum is comfortable near-term on the strength of its lead arrangement with a Japanese supplier plus the AXT deal, but flagged that given the rate of change in the demand vector 'that may not be true a quarter or two from now either' - more substrate help is likely needed if the vector continues.
quarterly_data.figure: AXT InP substrate deal signed in Q4; more substrate supply likely needed if demand vector continues

quarterly_data.signal: Technology roadmap view: silicon photonics is a viable solution at 1.6T and CW lasers are taking a significant portion of transceiver output, but at 3.2T silicon photonics 'loses some of its advantages' and Lumentum expects EMLs to come back in a meaningful way. Wupen Yuen added that in a supply-constrained environment customers will use whichever laser source they can get, so the EML-versus-CW mix is a supply/demand dynamic as much as a technical one. CPO remains the natural end state - optics placed directly on the substrate or interposer for maximum power efficiency through foundry-level advanced packaging.
quarterly_data.figure: SiPho viable at 1.6T; EML expected to return at 3.2T; CPO the end state via foundry advanced packaging

quarterly_data.signal: Competitive: on Chinese companies bringing new indium phosphide fabs to market, Hurlston said 'we obviously haven't seen any impact on our numbers as yet. I don't expect there to be any impact,' citing EML differentiation, high/mid-power laser differentiation for NPO and CPO, and an ability to price up even in CW because tight spec consistency drives superior customer transceiver yields. He cautioned that some Chinese laser suppliers are not yet delivering into the market.
quarterly_data.figure: no impact seen from new Chinese InP fabs; price premium sustained

quarterly_data.signal: Adjacent businesses: industrial lasers and cable access strengthened quarter-over-quarter. Within industrial lasers, increased adoption of ultrafast lasers targeting high-density PCB via drilling that supports advanced AI XPU boards and 1.6T optical modules. In 3D sensing, Lumentum has visibility to an expanding set of applications expected to drive growth in upcoming product cycles with its primary customer.
quarterly_data.figure: ultrafast lasers for AI XPU board / 1.6T module PCB via drilling; expanding 3D sensing pipeline

quarterly_data.signal: Named by AOI management on its Q2 FY2026 call as one of the very few suppliers able to serve the high-power CPO laser market: AOI, Lumentum, Coherent and Broadcom are all 'invest[ing] huge money' in laser capacity, yet 'even combined... it's still very tough to meet the customer demand in the next few years'. Sizing: CPO/ELSFP needs a 300mW laser (vs 70mW for 800G, 100mW for 1.6T) with ~6x larger die, so the industry laser market must grow 8-10x; DWDM ELSFP carries 40-50% worse yield loss than 1310nm, and laser equipment takes 21-24 months from order to high-volume output. AOI states only AOI, Lumentum and Coherent can hit acceptable DWDM CPO laser / CPO module yields.
quarterly_data.figure: Industry high-power laser capacity must grow 8-10x for CPO; 21-24 month equipment lead time

quarterly_data.signal: In July, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston indicated that the supply shortage of indium phosphide could be even more severe than that of memory, with multiple areas of supply constraint outlined (cited by Sivers Semiconductors)

By product type, Components revenue was $2,005.6 million (+79.7% Y/Y from $1,116.3 million) and Systems revenue was $1,008.4 million (+90.7% Y/Y from $528.7 million).

quarterly_data.signal: New company guidance given at the conference, not on the Q4 FY2026 earnings call: 'in 2028, we figure that we can now deliver $40 of earnings power' (fiscal 2028). The driver is OCS - since the last earnings call Lumentum's largest OCS customer 'has taken up their orders very significantly', producing 'a huge uptick in our order book and the order rate'. Hurlston: 'The OCS numbers have come up a lot since our last earnings call, and that really gives us a lot of confidence, given the margin profile of that good, to substantially take up where we think our earnings power will be in 2028, in our fiscal 2028' - a take-up he described as running against where all the sell-side analysts had the company.
quarterly_data.figure: $40 of earnings power in fiscal 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Hurlston pushed back on the assumption that Lumentum OCS equals Google: 'the breadth of customer engagement is very high on OCS. We started with customers other than Google... we actually have customers that were much more substantial than Google in our early rounds of shipments.' One of the more interesting emerging use cases is deploying an OCS inside the rack itself, one per rack, to route around GPUs or TPUs that have failed or are overloaded - a surprising number of GPUs in a data center fail, and a compute model can represent '$20, 30, $40 million of compute time'. At the lead customer the number of OCSs per torus is also going up. As a result the $8 billion OCS TAM Lumentum published at OFC 'now looks like it's significantly under called', and a new, significantly higher TAM number is expected at the next OFC in March of next year. OCS has power and optical-loss advantages over an electrical switch and Hurlston expects it to be 'one of the largest growth drivers in the company'.
quarterly_data.figure: $20, 30, $40 million of compute time at risk per model; $8 billion OCS TAM described as significantly under called

quarterly_data.signal: New EML economics and share math. Moving from 100G to 200G EML gives 'about a 2x uplift in price' - ASPs roughly double - and 200G lasers arrive at the 1.6T node. At 200G there is 'very little competition': Broadcom is a supplier of 200G EMLs, Lumentum is the other large supplier, and management sees no other entrants soon. On mix, EML-based transceivers are 'probably 70%-80%' of the 800G market but are expected to be only '40%-50% of the market at 1.6T' as silicon photonics takes share, so raw EML units go up while share comes down. At 3.2T Lumentum's transceiver engineers say 'silicon photonics again runs out of steam', producing 'a double whammy' where both EML unit numbers and EML share rise. Hurlston also framed the yield argument behind the price premium: the tolerance of the laser sets transceiver yield more than anything else, so a higher laser price 'more than makes up for itself in the high yields'.
quarterly_data.figure: 100G to 200G EML about a 2x uplift in price; EML share of transceivers 70%-80% at 800G falling to 40%-50% at 1.6T; share rises again at 3.2T

quarterly_data.signal: First run-rate history given for the Cloud Light transceiver business: acquired doing 'roughly $75 million a quarter', revenue then fell 'below $50 million, a quarterly run rate of 40 to 50' on quality problems that largest customer Google complained about; after retooling engineering it recovered to 'about a $100 million quarterly run rate' and is 'now running well over $200 million a quarter', expected to grow considerably throughout 2027. At the 1.6T transition Lumentum got to the head of the curve on signal integrity and is 'now shipping ahead of great competitors like InnoLight and Coherent' (Eoptolink also named), first to market on a lot of its SKUs. The unresolved problem is gross margin - still below the top competitors - which management plans to attack on the manufacturing side entering calendar 2027, while conceding it may never match InnoLight or Eoptolink.
quarterly_data.figure: Cloud Light about $75 million a quarter at acquisition, below $50 million trough (40 to 50 run rate), back to about $100 million, now well over $200 million a quarter

quarterly_data.signal: NPO timing moved materially since the earnings call: 'prior to our last earnings call, we probably thought that it was going to be a late 2028 into early 2029 event... It seems like now it's a late 2027 into early 2028 event', because customers competing with NVIDIA concluded they need to deploy a lot more optics and to do so sooner. Hurlston called the near-term NPO opportunity larger than the CPO opportunity, with a higher adoption rate of optical lanes than NVIDIA's, and said NPO customers are requiring Lumentum to ship the entire ELS rather than bare laser chips. The consequence is capacity: NPO 'is going to put a lot of pressure on that Greensboro fab', Lumentum needs a 'next leg of the stool' and is trying to lock up NPO business now to fill Greensboro and more, but would require an NVIDIA-style commitment before funding further capacity. NVIDIA underwrote Greensboro with a long-term agreement characterised as a multibillion-dollar deal plus an investment that helped Lumentum buy, equip and outfit the fab, acquired early calendar 2026 and not operational until early calendar 2028; the team running it was inherited from Qorvo, and qualification at NVIDIA itself took a year.
quarterly_data.figure: NPO pulled in from a late 2028 into early 2029 event to a late 2027 into early 2028 event; Greensboro acquired early calendar 2026, operational early calendar 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Geopolitical sizing not given on the call: Lumentum is 'probably correctly' viewed as a net beneficiary of a U.S. move to ban Chinese transceivers, but 'the Chinese transceiver suppliers make 70% of the transceivers in the U.S. market', so cutting that off entirely without a thoughtful, industry-coordinated phase-in 'would be a challenge' for the whole hyperscaler industry; Lumentum could mobilize relatively quickly, as could Coherent, but it would take time. The reverse risk is tit-for-tat curtailment of Chinese sub-component supply - substrates, isolators and other raw materials Lumentum currently relies on - against which its manufacturing footprint in Thailand, in China itself and in the United Kingdom (a safe harbour on substrates) is the hedge.
quarterly_data.figure: Chinese transceiver suppliers make 70% of the transceivers in the U.S. market

quarterly_data.signal: Kathy Ta sized the optical bandwidth step-up per interconnect tier for the first time: if Data Center Interconnect / telecom is a 1x multiple, scale-across and scale-out are each roughly 10x DCI; the first instance of CPO going to scale-up, starting in the second half of 2027, is 'probably 3x to 4x above the 10x that we are seeing for scale-out', and when all of scale-up goes optical it is 'a full 10x above the 10x of scale-out', with scale-in another 10x multiple beyond that. Wupen Yuen framed the same ladder as scale-across 1, scale-out 10, scale-up 100, scale-in 1,000, and positioned Lumentum as 'going all the way from scale across to scale out, to scale up, and later to scale in'.
quarterly_data.figure: scale-across and scale-out each about 10x DCI; scale-up CPO 3x to 4x above the 10x of scale-out from the second half of 2027; full optical scale-up a full 10x above scale-out; scale-in another 10x

quarterly_data.signal: Post-earnings supply update: the supply-demand gap is 'still extending' and Lumentum is 'still short everywhere' - DML short, CW laser short. Yuen does not see the shortage going away in 2027; the industry forecasts scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027 while laser supply does not catch up, and 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x increase of demand, so the laser supply-demand gap does not close within the next couple of years. Lumentum is still allocating capacity, in some cases on pricing and expedite fees, to serve the most profitable opportunities, and 'all the deals we are making today are equal or higher pricing than the escalated pricing that we already had before' - management's own read that the gap persists.
quarterly_data.figure: scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027; 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x demand increase; gap does not close within the next couple of years

quarterly_data.signal: Yuen reframed optical scale-up as an industry-wide story rather than the single-customer CPO story assumed at OFC: to serve 2028 optical scale-up volume the industry needs both CPO and NPO approaches, and by volume 'CPO will be half of the market. NPO is the other half of the market' - roughly 50/50. On the content Lumentum sells, CPO is 'an exclusive external light source market'; half of NPO also goes external light source (ELS) and the remaining roughly 25% of the overall market is still being debated between integrated light source (ILS) and ELS, with more and more movement toward ELS because the optical engine sits so close to the accelerator heat source that an integrated laser becomes the reliability-limiting factor. Even the ILS case will not use pluggable-class lasers: an NPO engine '1 inch by half an inch' packs 6.4T versus half an iPhone for a 1.6T module today, so fewer but higher-power lasers are required and the entire NPO/CPO application moves to '120, 150 milliwatt and above', not the traditional 70 milliwatt pluggable laser. Chinese CW laser supply chatter is aimed at that pluggable market, not this one.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO half and NPO half of the optical scale-up market; ILS about 25% of the overall market; NPO engine 1 inch by half an inch packing 6.4T vs a 1.6T module today; 120, 150 milliwatt and above vs traditional 70 milliwatt

quarterly_data.signal: Three-wave ultra-high-power (UHP) laser capacity ramp laid out for the first time: wave one is the San Jose fab, ramping today with line of sight through 2027; wave two is the U.K. fab, which 'will come in in second quarter 2027' and continues ramping through 2028; wave three is the Greensboro fab, starting to ramp in 'second quarter 2028 or mid 2028'. All three are on schedule and the biggest variable is customer qualification timing - Lumentum must submit a PCN for the customer to qualify the product, and accelerating that qualification can pull the ramp in. Capacity is additive rather than reallocated: a new clean room in the U.K. fitted with 'the latest and greatest state-of-the-art equipment', and the added capacity is '6-inch capable', so current telecom and scale-across products are not sacrificed - 'by and large, we do not sacrifice. We add.'
quarterly_data.figure: San Jose ramping through 2027; U.K. fab second quarter 2027 ramping through 2028; Greensboro second quarter 2028 or mid 2028; new 6-inch capable capacity

quarterly_data.signal: Kathy Ta quantified the first ELS win announced on the Q4 FY2026 call: it is with the existing CPO customer, it covers only 'a relatively small portion of their ELS total demand', first ELS shipments are expected in the second half of calendar 2027, and Lumentum estimates 'maybe 15%-20% of their fleet is about the right amount of their share that we think that we will win'. She expects a bigger ELS share opportunity in NPO because the majority of the NPO opportunity looks ELS rather than ILS, and many of those ELS customers want Lumentum to supply the complete ELS module rather than only laser chips. No NPO win has been announced yet, but management expects to announce a first NPO customer 'in the next handful of months'.
quarterly_data.figure: about 15%-20% of the lead CPO customer's ELS fleet; first ELS shipments in the second half of calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: First OCS content metric management has given: investors can model 'a 1.5 port to one XPU attach rate' for the major applications, with the puts and takes from new topologies (back end of network, fewer hops) netting out to roughly the same attach rate. On sizing, the $8 billion OCS TAM Lumentum put on a slide six months ago now looks low: besides the largest customer's own success in the market, OCS is moving into serious R&D for tray-level / in-rack dynamic partitioning (a customer may not want a fixed 576 XPUs in a cluster) and for resiliency network applications that route around underperforming accelerators, which management says gives visibility to a lot more OCS being required by the late 2028 / early 2029 timeframe.
quarterly_data.figure: 1.5 port to one XPU OCS attach rate; $8 billion OCS TAM seen with upside; 576 XPUs in a cluster; late 2028, early 2029 timeframe

quarterly_data.signal: Competitive read on high-power CPO/NPO lasers: Yuen named Coherent as the single competitor - 'we see the one competitor, right, who is Coherent' - and said Lumentum is 'really not seeing anybody else in this high-power laser area'. He described why the part is hard (power, RIN noise, linewidth and mode hop all have to be achieved simultaneously at volume with good yield, and mode hop is the biggest problem with today's silicon photonics lasers), noted Lumentum is already ramping these lasers and seeing good real data, and then said the industry needs a second source: from a customer's point of view Coherent would need to be ramping 'sometime in 2027... Probably second half' to support the scale-up build in 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: Coherent second source needed around the second half of 2027 to support the 2028 scale-up ramp

quarterly_data.signal: CW LASER YIELD NOW ABOVE EML, PRICING SIMILAR: Wupen Yuen (President of Global Business Units) said 'our CW laser yield has climbed up to be higher than EMLs' and that CW pricing 'is similar to EMLs'; with the die shrunk closer to EML size, 'the margin profile is not going to be as good as EMLs, but pretty close with CW lasers', so Lumentum's past hesitance to put more CW lasers out is 'gradually diminishing'. (The Q4 FY2026 call said the CW-EML margin gap had closed considerably; it did not compare CW yield with EML.)
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q2 2026 results (quarter ended December 27, 2025; non-GAAP): record revenue of $665.5 million, at the high end of guidance, with over 65% year-over-year growth - a company record for the second reporting period in a row. Non-GAAP gross margin 42.5% (up 310 basis points sequentially, 820 basis points year-on-year on utilization, increased pricing on select products and mix led by data center laser chips); non-GAAP operating margin 25.2% (up 1,730 basis points year-on-year); non-GAAP EPS $1.67; GAAP net income $78.2 million. Components revenue $443.7 million (up 17% sequentially, 68% year-on-year) on laser chips, laser assemblies and inline subsystems; Systems revenue $221.8 million (up 43% sequentially, 60% year-on-year). Pump laser revenue grew over 90% year-over-year to a record, and narrow linewidth laser assembly shipments grew for the eighth consecutive quarter; industrial end-market shipments were roughly flat sequentially. quarterly_data.figure: revenue $665.5 million (over 65% YoY); non-GAAP gross margin 42.5%; operating margin 25.2%; EPS $1.67; Components $443.7 million (+68%); Systems $221.8 million (+60%); pump lasers over 90% YoY; CapEx $84 million

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q3 2026 guidance (CFO Wajid Ali, non-GAAP): net revenue $780 to $830 million; the $805 million midpoint would be a new all-time quarterly record and 'represents an impressive 85% plus year-over-year increase' (CEO). Price increases start flowing through in the March guide; the CEO called the effect 'relatively modest.'

quarterly_data.signal: CPO / ultra-high-power (UHP) lasers: Lumentum 'secured an additional multi-$100 million purchase order for ultra-high-power lasers that support optical scale-out applications,' with shipments for this order in 2027 ('clicking in in the first half of 2027'). Initial CPO orders remain on track for a material UHP shipment inflection in the second half of calendar 2026, pegged at 'somewhere around $50 million in the fourth calendar quarter. Perhaps more.' The ramp spans multiple customers and is hitting faster than forecast last quarter: 'We're very much sold out in our powered laser fab.' Hurlston cited the 400 milliwatts power level ('not something that many people can do') and reliability proven in subsea applications as the basis for broader CPO customer engagement.
quarterly_data.figure: additional multi-$100 million UHP laser purchase order (shipments first half of 2027); around $50 million UHP/CPO revenue in the fourth calendar quarter; 400 milliwatts lasers

quarterly_data.signal: New growth vectors: Lumentum has 'a clear line of sight into the broader external light source (ELS) market' - pluggable ELS modules rather than standalone laser chips - which Hurlston sized at 'somewhere around two, two and a half times content gain from a revenue standpoint as compared to just our lasers,' at decent margins, and which diversifies the customer base as new partners adopt next-generation scale-out architectures. Optical scale-up is named a fourth growth driver: 'By late calendar 2027, we would expect our first scale-up CPO shipments replacing longer copper connections,' with Lumentum in design-in cycles using UHP lasers and ELS modules. Yuen called scale-up 'a brand new market that didn't exist before.' Given the scale-up opportunity, Lumentum is 'in active negotiations with leading customers to offset our capital requirements in exchange for long-term supply assurances.'
quarterly_data.figure: ELS module around two, two and a half times content gain vs lasers alone; first scale-up CPO shipments by late calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity: the indium phosphide wafer fab capacity 'remains at a premium, fully allocated.' Lumentum front-loaded its 40% expansion target (all at Sagamihara), delivering 'a little bit north of 20% in the December alone,' with 'another 20% to go over the next couple of quarters' and likely a little better than 40% overall. It now has line of sight to further capacity through the second half of calendar 2026 into early 2027 via Sagamihara, the Caswell, United Kingdom fab and the second Japan fab at Takao. Management said new fab capacity 'by, you know, acquisition or something of that nature' is an active investigation. Back-end factory capacity is also a significant constraint: Lumentum has 'pivoted from a manufacturing strategy to really look at more contract manufacturing,' is stepping up its Nava, Thailand site, clearing some China factory footprint for the most important SKUs, and hired a new back-end operations leader (from Jabil) to move more products to contract manufacturers.
quarterly_data.figure: 40% InP capacity expansion front-loaded (north of 20% in the December quarter; another 20% over the next couple of quarters); more capacity from Sagamihara, Caswell and Takao

Hurlston: 'All of our capacity, just to be very clear on EML, is spoken for in these LTAs. Concrete measure: Coherent produced about 80% MORE indium phosphide lasers in the June quarter than a year earlier — those lasers feed 800G and 1.6T transceiver shipments in the current quarter, so management expects data-center revenue growth this quarter to EXCEED 80% YoY. Engagement intensity with customers on CPO and/or NPO 'has really gone up over the last three to six months', with almost every large strategic customer running a CPO or NPO project (some both). Content per socket is COMPARABLE between CPO and NPO — 'just a different attach point' — because Coherent supplies the laser, external laser module, isolators, polarization-maintaining fiber, full fiber-attach kit assembly and SiPho PICs rather than a single ingredient. quarterly_data.signal: Six-inch indium phosphide ramp running ahead of plan: Coherent significantly increased InP production in Q2 and is on track to double internal InP production by the fourth quarter of calendar 2026. Current-quarter wafer starts are already at 80% of the doubling target, after wafer starts more than quadrupled from the September quarter to the December quarter; a wafer start takes about six months to become a transceiver shipment, so the benefit starts this quarter and builds over coming quarters. Production is ramping in parallel at Sherman, Texas and Yarfala, Sweden, with EMLs, CW lasers and photodiodes all in production on six-inch and six-inch yields exceeding three-inch yields. A six-inch wafer produces more than four times as many chips at less than half the cost; almost all capacity being added is six-inch, about half of capacity will be six-inch by the end of calendar 2026, and plans go well beyond doubling in following years. Coherent has multiple six-inch InP substrate suppliers and has secured committed substrate supply supporting the doubling; management called Coherent the world's only producer of six-inch indium phosphide.
quarterly_data.figure: wafer starts at 80% of the capacity-doubling target; about six months from wafer start to transceiver shipment

quarterly_data.signal: Management does not foresee indium phosphide supply and demand getting back in balance this calendar year or next calendar year, and, given customer forecasts for the InP laser supply they need for scale-up, sees a possible 'very sustained long period of supply-demand imbalance on indium phosphide'; customer demand absorbs all planned capacity 'and then some'. The majority of Coherent's InP lasers are internally sourced and the internal share is expected to grow, but external EML supply increased sequentially in Q2 and is expected to increase again through long-term partnerships with key external suppliers (kept for customer and supply-chain resiliency reasons). Coherent is seeing higher input pricing on externally sourced EMLs, which management said is offset by its internal InP ramp for a net positive, and it continues to optimize its own pricing in the strong demand environment.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Coherent recently secured an 'exceptionally large' purchase order from a market-leading AI data center customer (not named) for a CPO solution that includes its new high-power CW laser, which began sampling last year; a key factor in the customer's choice was that the laser is produced on the six-inch InP line in Sherman, Texas (US-based manufacturing). Initial revenue is expected toward the end of calendar 2026, with a more significant contribution next calendar year and beyond. The solution will initially be deployed in scale-out and is expected to lead to scale-up deployments over time. On top of transceiver demand, Coherent is ramping InP capacity to support the high-power CW laser demand ahead, and it has engagements with multiple other customers for InP- and 200G VCSEL-based solutions for CPO and MPO applications.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: Management views CPO as additive: pluggable transceivers remain the dominant form factor in scale-across and scale-out through at least the rest of the decade, CPO deploys first in scale-out, but the big CPO growth is driven by scale-up, which management believes 'will dwarf the opportunity in scale-out' and be 'orders of magnitude larger', all incremental TAM because the in-rack scale-up network is 100% electrical today. There are very active, deep CPO design-win engagements for scale-up across multiple customers, and management does not consider scale-up CPO years out. Coherent plans to supply scale-up both at the component level (high-power CW lasers, detectors, fiber optical cable) and at higher levels (external laser sources, including pluggable laser sources for the front panel, and CPO module assemblies).
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: OCS (optical circuit switch on Coherent's non-mechanical liquid crystal technology): backlog grew sequentially in Q2 and Coherent now has over 10 customer engagements; shipments and backlog include 64 by 64 and 320 by 320 system sizes, with most backlog weighted toward the larger size. OCS revenue is expected to grow sequentially this quarter and ramp through this calendar year and into next year, with Coherent 100% focused on ramping production. Applications are broadening from spine/redundancy and scale-out uses to the DC portion of the network and to scale-up; the market sized about a year ago at about $2 billion by the end of the decade was likely undersized and, if reassessed now, would be well above $2 billion.
quarterly_data.figure: over 10 customer engagements; addressable market well above $2 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Communications (DCI, scale-across and traditional telecom): extremely strong demand for data center interconnect products, including ZR and ZR+ coherent transceivers and lasers and other components sold to system OEMs, with DCI growing faster than the overall communications business and backlog growing. Coherent recently secured a significant multiyear design win with a leading DCI OEM (not named) that uses its industry-first uncooled three-pin micropump solution. The new multi-rail platform, which lets network operators get more traffic through existing optical infrastructure, has design wins and orders, with revenue contribution expected to start in the second half of calendar 2026. Communications is expected to grow sequentially in the March and June quarters.

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 capital expenditures were $154 million versus $104 million in the prior quarter and $106 million a year ago, and are expected to increase sequentially over the remainder of fiscal 2026 as Coherent rapidly expands capacity for data center and communications demand. Beyond InP, it is expanding transceiver assembly and test capacity: a second facility in Penang, Malaysia was opened, and Vietnam, which already makes transceiver components, is starting to build transceivers; DCI and telecom capacity is also being expanded. Coherent uses outsourcing partners and keeps in-house only what gives a technology or cost-structure advantage.

quarterly_data.signal: FY2025 (calendar year) group revenue GBP 97.3 million. Photonics revenue rose 15% to GBP 57.1 million, "driven by continued growth in AI and data center related markets... as well as the funding releases for certain U.S. military and defense programs." Wireless revenue fell 40% to GBP 40.1 million on macro/tariff uncertainty and mobile handset softness, "with some end customer requirements met from existing inventory." Adjusted EBITDA of GBP 3.2 million was "a direct reflection of the low utilization of our manufacturing footprint." The first half was weak (tariff uncertainty, handset inventory build, delayed military and defense funding); conditions improved through H2 as wireless customer inventory depleted and U.S. defense budget was released.

quarterly_data.signal: FY2026 outlook: "Trading in Q1 2026 was in line with management expectations, reflecting strong demand across all of our core segments... we expect full-year revenue growth for 2026 exceeding 20% year-on-year. This is expected to result in high single digit to low double digit adjusted EBITDA position." Named growth drivers: indium phosphide photonic products for AI compute and data center deployments, VCSEL and wireless products for consumer smartphones, and ongoing aerospace and defense strength.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue growth >20% YoY; adjusted EBITDA "high single digit to low double digit" (unit not specified on the call)

quarterly_data.signal: InP demand for AI optics is accelerating: "In the last year, we have seen market demand from these indium phosphide solutions significantly increase due to the exponential growth in AI... The nature of the supply they're demanding is very much in the here and now. This is a live market opportunity." On the order book: "We have strong order book visibility going into the second half." Management frames InP as the crucial enabler of the ultra-fast optical and wireless data communications that data centers rely on, with IQE positioned by decades of InP epitaxy experience, and says hyperscale AI and data centers are "a massive opportunity for us across our materials portfolio, but especially in relation to indium phosphide."

We are working closely with our suppliers to mitigate any kind of indium phosphide shortages that we are seeing. Ultimately, the main component here will be to dual source or to increase really our sourcing capabilities and ensuring that we are just not reliant on one supplier alone." IQE is monitoring it jointly with suppliers and customers. On its own epi capacity, by contrast: "Right now, we are not seeing any capacity constraints as mentioned in our revenue outlook" - the existing asset base can support the 2026, 2027 and 2028 demand increase "without significantly increasing our fixed cost base."

On converting GaAs lines to InP: "Our tool set is flexible to some degree. We can certainly transfer or convert capacity from our technology to the next. That kind of conversion would again need to be tied to discrete customer demand and visibility to that, because obviously it does come with downtime of the tools and also CapEx commitments." On Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy: "We are monitoring demand very closely, and as mentioned, we are converting capacities if and when that demand materializes." Additional MOCVD tools would come via LTA, customer co-funding, or tool consignment - "any kind of capacity expansion or addition of tools will need to come with customer commitments." Wafer-diameter transitions (4->6 inch, 6->8 inch) are customer-driven, with no company-wide push.

quarterly_data.signal: Balance sheet transformed after year end. FY2025 closed with cash and cash equivalents of GBP 15.7 million, adjusted net debt of GBP 31.5 million, and a working capital inflow of GBP 11.2 million. The GBP 81 million fundraise - GBP 45 million from MACOM (GBP 30 million cash plus GBP 15 million of convertible loan notes), with the remainder from existing shareholders - closed the morning of this results call. Proceeds fully repay the HSBC revolving credit facility and redeem existing loan notes, "leaving us without bank debt," with net cash inflow to IQE of around GBP 27.9 million. Management does "not foresee any additional fundraisers in the future" absent a large customer-backed capacity expansion. The 18-month strategic review - which assessed options from a sale of Taiwan up to a full sale of the company - concluded that staying independent creates the best shareholder value.
quarterly_data.figure: GBP 81M raised (GBP 45M from MACOM); net cash inflow ~GBP 27.9M; FY25 cash GBP 15.7M; FY25 adjusted net debt GBP 31.5M

IQE is a heavily fixed-cost business, so incremental volume falls through hard to EBITDA; a mix weighted toward InP and GaN carries better margin than commodity VCSEL/wireless.

One month later GF announced SCALE (Silicon Photonics Co-packaged Advanced Light Engine), the industry's FIRST OCI-MSA-capable complete optical module platform for NPO/CPO, with specs exceeding MSA requirements (natively broadband fiber coupling minimizing insertion loss). The implied exit rate is roughly $350 million per quarter, and management reaffirmed the long-term model of 30-plus percent year-over-year growth for this end market into 2027 and beyond.

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon photonics revenue reported within comms infrastructure and data center is now expected to MORE THAN DOUBLE in 2026 versus the prior year. GF secured 7 new optical networking design wins in Q2 across both pluggable transceiver suppliers and major hyperscaler and networking players, and is actively engaged with 4 OF THE TOP 5 optical transceiver players. Pluggables contribute the vast majority of silicon photonics revenue today. High-volume manufacturing of 200-gig-per-lane technology is underway, 400-gig capability has already been demonstrated, and the multiyear roadmap advances module enablement to 1.6T, 3.2T and beyond. GF has more than 40 silicon photonics customers, and CEO Tim Breen said GF is on track and potentially ahead of the growth targets set for end-2028 through 2030. He also cited an expectation that 70% of data center links will be optical by 2030, calling that 'perhaps even conservative' given scale-up as well as scale-out penetration.
quarterly_data.figure: Silicon photonics revenue to more than double in 2026; 7 new design wins in Q2; engaged with 4 of top 5 transceiver players; >40 SiPho customers; 200G/lane in HVM, 400G/lane demonstrated

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE, described as the industry's first OCI MSA compatible solution for near and co-packaged optics, has 7 ACTIVE ENGAGEMENTS with leading companies. GF taped out a SCALE-related design win in Q2 and expects to tape out another in Q3. Management reiterated a consistent timeline: the NPO ramp BEGINS IN 2027 and the CPO ramp BEGINS IN 2028. Because near and co-packaged optics are built on a common photonic IC - an EIC bonded to a PIC with a micro-optic and a fiber-attached unit - and differ mainly in that NPO is bonded to the board while CPO sits within the package (plus SerDes architecture differences), GF expects to benefit regardless of which form factor customers adopt. Many customers are pursuing both, with NPO ramping sooner. Breen attributed the sudden industry interest in NPO to SerDes synergies that make the system transition smaller than a jump straight to full CPO, and expects pluggables, NPO and CPO all to coexist in the data center.
quarterly_data.figure: 7 active SCALE engagements; 1 SCALE tape-out in Q2 and another expected in Q3; NPO ramp begins 2027, CPO ramp begins 2028

quarterly_data.signal: GF entered a letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for a $300 MILLION award to accelerate next-generation silicon photonics technologies in the U.S. The funding supports three components: continued PIC-level innovation and improved modulator technology to reach 400-gig per lane and beyond; NEW MATERIALS to be introduced into the system - management named barium titanate, thin-film lithium niobate and indium phosphide; and packaging capability and capacity for the integrated optical engines needed for near and co-packaged optics, building directly on the SCALE platform. Management said the endorsement came from the world's top XPU providers, hyperscalers, AI connectivity leaders and ecosystem partners.
quarterly_data.figure: $300M U.S. Department of Commerce letter of intent for next-generation silicon photonics

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon germanium is OVERSUBSCRIBED THROUGHOUT 2027 and, notably, GF's SiGe business is LARGER THAN ITS SILICON PHOTONICS BUSINESS TODAY. GF secured multiple new SiGe TIA and driver design wins across networking customers in the quarter. The growth has two compounding drivers: the shift to optical networking itself, and the fact that what could previously be done in CMOS at 50-gig and 100-gig per lane cannot be done at 200-gig and definitely not at 400-gig per lane, forcing transimpedance amplifiers and increasingly the drivers out into high-performance analog processes like SiGe. High-performance analog also appears in near and co-packaged optics depending on architecture. GF is expanding SiGe capacity at Burlington, Vermont and qualifying 300-millimeter SiGe in Singapore for additional capacity, better economics and higher fT/fMAX performance. The SiGe lineage traces to IBM Microelectronics, which invented SiGe and is part of GF today.
quarterly_data.figure: SiGe oversubscribed throughout 2027; SiGe business larger than silicon photonics today; Vermont capacity expanding, 300mm SiGe qualifying in Singapore

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity strategy is a structural advantage: GF is adding capacity WITHIN ITS EXISTING FAB FOOTPRINT rather than building new fabs, which management contrasted with competitors on longer lead times. Breen said GF 'could 10x our photonics capacity within our current 4 walls' globally on its long-term plan. Q2 utilization was in the high 80s, leaving about 10 points of headroom to grow into with installed capacity. Confidence in bringing capacity online plus factory productivity improvements was cited as a direct contributor to raising the full-year CID outlook. On competition in silicon photonics, Breen said customers are coming to GF saying they do not have enough capacity secured and want more, partly to mitigate geopolitical risk, and he sees no customer-concentration concern given 40-plus customers.
quarterly_data.figure: Photonics capacity expandable ~10x within existing fabs; Q2 utilization high-80s with ~10 points of headroom

quarterly_data.signal: GF implemented PRICING INCREASES in partnership with customers across several technology corridors during Q2, following what management called constructive conversations. The adjustments will be reflected in revenue COMMENCING IN 2027, with magnitude varying by end market and technology based on differentiated value, supply/demand dynamics and inflationary absorption. GF will continue assessing 2027 pricing through the second half of 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: Price increases agreed across several technology corridors, revenue impact commencing 2027

quarterly_data.signal: GF launched Quantum Technology Solutions in May 2026, a dedicated team aimed at taking the quantum industry from prototypes to high-volume production. The strategy is qubit-agnostic across superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, topological and spin modalities, using the FDX platform as a cryogenic CMOS foundation and extending advanced packaging into the cryogenic regime for 3D heterogeneous integration. GF is working with 8 of the world's leading quantum computing players including PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Quantum Motion plus endorsements from the quantum arms of large hyperscalers, and has already begun 4 new customer-specific engagements in the three months since launch. The effort is anchored by an expected $375 MILLION grant from the U.S. Department of Commerce. Over the next 1 to 3 years quantum revenue comes largely through engineering engagements booked in technology services, with manufacturing-services revenue ramping toward the end of the decade. Several quantum players are working on the photonics side of their solutions, which maps directly onto GF's silicon photonics roadmap.
quarterly_data.figure: $375M expected U.S. Department of Commerce quantum grant; 8 leading quantum players engaged; 4 new customer engagements in 3 months

quarterly_data.signal: IP, software and custom silicon: GF completed the acquisition of the Synopsys ARC processor IP Solutions business in June, adding CPU, DSP, NPU and RISC-V technologies, a software development toolkit and application-specific processor design capability - over 150 patents, 300 existing customers and 400 R&D engineers. Combined with MIPS, this lets GF engage customers earlier in the design cycle for edge AI and on-device inference in automotive, industrial and robotics. Full-year 2026 technology services contribution from MIPS plus ARC was RAISED to $100-120 million from a prior $60-100 million, skewed roughly one third Q3 and two thirds Q4, and technology services revenue is now expected toward the high end of the 10-12% of total revenue range with gross margin significantly above corporate targets. Design wins in the quarter included 3 strategic chiplet wins with Lockheed Martin on FinFET and FDX, an expanded FinFET win with Microchip, a first-ever PMIC design win with MediaTek on the BCD platform, an ADAS radar tape-out for Bosch on FDX, and a new microLED display backplane win for augmented reality wearables at a leading hyperscaler.
quarterly_data.figure: Technology services contribution raised to $100M-$120M for 2026 (from $60M-$100M); ARC adds 150 patents, 300 customers, 400 R&D engineers

quarterly_data.signal: End-market split and the memory-shortage read-across: smart mobile devices were ~36% of Q2 revenue, up 15% sequentially but down 6% year over year, and are now expected to DECLINE BY A LOW-TEENS PERCENTAGE in 2026 because 2026 handset forecasts have been cut meaningfully on continued memory pricing and associated shortages. Automotive was ~19% of revenue, down 13% sequentially and 10% year over year on customer-led shipment timing, but full-year low-double-digit growth is still expected weighted to Q4. Home and industrial IoT was ~19% of revenue, up 30% sequentially and 10% year over year - its fastest year-over-year growth since 2022 - and the full-year outlook was raised to 10-15% growth from mid-single digits, partly because mobile customers reallocated demand into IoT connectivity applications. GF credited a deliberately flexible manufacturing footprint for reusing capacity to capture data-center upside as mobile weakened.
quarterly_data.figure: Smart mobile ~36% of revenue, FY2026 down low teens on memory shortage; automotive ~19%; IoT ~19%, FY2026 raised to 10-15% growth

quarterly_data.signal: Cash and capital returns: Q2 cash flow from operations was $405 million and capex net of government grant proceeds was $408 million (roughly 23% of revenue), leaving adjusted free cash flow at negative $3 million as previously guided. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were approximately $3.3 billion against $1.1 billion of total debt, with a $1 billion revolving credit facility undrawn. GF paid its first-ever quarterly cash dividend of $0.12 per share on July 14 and declared another $0.12 per share payable October 9, 2026. Approximately $100 million remains under the share repurchase authorization; the stated objective is to return up to 50% of trailing-twelve-month non-IFRS adjusted free cash flow after investments over time.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 OCF $405M; capex $408M (~23% of revenue); adjusted FCF -$3M; $3.3B cash and securities; first-ever dividend $0.12/share

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Tim Breen on the silicon photonics growth targets: 'the industry adoption needed to reach those targets has already happened. So I think we now have very limited adoption risk baked into that.' The constraint is now supply, not demand - 'All indicators right now from a demand point of view are flashing kind of bright green relative to those targets... we see much more demand than we can supply out of our current install base, so we will definitely be accelerating that.' Pluggables alone get GF 'pretty much all the way' to the first milestone, with NPO rollout already picking up steam on top. The upside case is co-packaged optics: if CPO sees really broad adoption in the latter part of the period GF 'could blow past those targets materially', because CPO is the technology for the scale-up transition and 'you are replacing 10x the links of scale-out with those solutions, so you are not going to see a linear growth story'.
quarterly_data.figure: co-packaged optics replaces 10x the links of scale-out

quarterly_data.signal: First photonics customer count disclosed: 'We have more than 40 customers in photonics today, and that number keeps growing as players really invest in their optical roadmap.' Breen added that 'everyone who was touting copper two years ago has either launched an organic or inorganic effort to get into optical'. On the form-factor transition, near-package optics and co-packaged optic designs are 'even taping out in our fabs today' and are 'going into production in 2027 and 2028', while pluggable optical transceivers ramp strongly now; the NPO rollout is being led by 'many of the same players who are in pluggables today'. The core photonics platform roadmap runs from 100 gig per lane to 200 gig per lane to 400 gig per lane and beyond with new materials and modulators, paired with advanced packaging (hybrid bonding, fiber-to-chip attach) as the optical link moves closer to the XPU and switch ASIC.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 40 customers in photonics; NPO and CPO designs taping out today and going into production in 2027 and 2028; 100 gig per lane to 200 to 400 gig per lane roadmap

quarterly_data.signal: Breen put GF squarely in a supply-constrained posture for the next couple of years: 'We are clearly in a chasing supply moment today'; 'for the next couple of years, we will be more in a supply-constrained than a demand-constrained environment'. Job number one is ramping technologies GF already produces to higher volumes, and capex is going up again - 'We already are increasing our CapEx this year from last year. We'll be increasing further again next year' - with tool install and qualification speed, not demand, the thing that 'will gate or accelerate our growth going into next year'. Two new-cycle features: customers are co-investing financially alongside GF in the ramps ('customer skin in the game... they are willing to put capital to work'), and government partnerships provide tools that let GF 'accelerate CapEx at significant recovery rates that were not there in the past'.
quarterly_data.figure: capex increasing this year versus last year and increasing further again next year; supply-constrained, not demand-constrained, for the next couple of years

quarterly_data.signal: Progress against the long-term model GF 'laid out early this year': GF set targets for communication infrastructure and data center of '30% or in the 30s' and, per Breen, 'We are doing 60 in Q2' - well ahead of plan in that segment. Automotive is tracking in line with the long-term plan and IoT slightly ahead year to date. Breen said he does 'not see a demand constraint to meeting and exceeding that plan' and that the diversification across platforms 'may even make those numbers look a bit conservative'.
quarterly_data.figure: communication infrastructure and data center target of 30% or in the 30s versus doing 60 in Q2

quarterly_data.signal: Mobile mix and a new read-across on foundry tightness: GF was 'more than 50% mobile going back a couple of years', is 'down to the mid-30s today' and the long-term model takes it to 'the mid-20s', with absolute mobile revenue assumed relatively flat rather than growing. 2026 is a tough year in mobile but 'not as tough at the higher end', where GF has more of its exposure. The new behaviour is that handset customers are now booking forward supply: 'mobile companies were the first to the queue in COVID... Now they are worried about being late when the data center is the one pushing all the demand. You are seeing actually more visibility where they are actually still saying, I need my supply for 2027. I need my supply for 2028.'
quarterly_data.figure: mobile more than 50% of revenue a couple of years ago, mid-30s today, mid-20s in the long-term model; handset customers booking supply for 2027 and 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Quantum status update since the Q2 call: 'today we announced that we completed the deal that we announced earlier in the year with the government', a partnership that accelerates GF's investment in infrastructure, tooling and PDK enablement for the more exotic processes - compressing a plan Breen framed as 'What would it take to do those in 2 years instead of over 5, 6 years?'. He stressed the roadmap is not orthogonal to the rest of GF: the exotic materials being proven for quantum - thin-film lithium niobate and barium titanate - 'will be needed for the next generation of photonics', i.e. the next generation of photonic modulators. The platform rests on cryo-CMOS (conventional FDSOI CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin) for qubit readout, plus novel-material integration, advanced packaging and high-speed photonic interconnect.
quarterly_data.figure: government partnership compressing a 5, 6 year plan into 2 years; cryo-CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 headline results, with revenue, gross margin and EPS at or above the high end of guidance: revenue $1.83 billion, up 8% sequentially and flat year-over-year; gross profit $530 million (approximately 29% gross margin, up 300 basis points sequentially and 360 basis points year-over-year); operating profit $335 million at an 18.3% operating margin; net income approximately $310 million; diluted EPS $0.55. Non-wafer revenue (reticles, NRE, expedite fees) was approximately 12% of Q4 revenue. Full-year 2025: revenue approximately $6.791 billion (up 1%), approximately 2.3 million 300-millimeter equivalent wafers shipped (up 10%) at utilization of approximately 85%, gross margin 26.1%, operating margin 15.7%, diluted EPS $1.72 (up 10%), adjusted free cash flow $1.2 billion (a record). 2025 was the first full year in which more than 60% of revenue came from markets other than smart mobile devices. The Board authorized a share repurchase of up to $500 million.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue $1.83 billion (up 8% sequentially, flat year-over-year); gross margin approximately 29%; operating margin 18.3%; EPS $0.55; FY2025 revenue approximately $6.791 billion (up 1%)

quarterly_data.signal: End markets: communications infrastructure and data center (CID) was approximately 12% of Q4 revenue and 11% of full-year revenue; Q4 CID revenue, which includes silicon photonics, increased approximately 29% sequentially and 32% year-over-year - the fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit year-over-year growth, driven by SATCOM and optical networking. Full-year 2025 CID revenue grew 29%, well above the prior expectation of low-20s growth, and satellite communications exceeded $100 million. For 2026 management expects CID to outperform peers and achieve over 30% year-on-year revenue growth. Automotive was approximately 23% of Q4 revenue and a record $1.4 billion for 2025 (up approximately 17%); automotive plus CID were about $2.2 billion, a record one third of 2025 revenue, up from approximately 27% the year prior. Smart mobile devices were approximately 36% of Q4 revenue and fell 12% in 2025 on GF-initiated one-time pricing adjustments with a small number of dual-sourced mobile customers; 2026 smart mobile is expected to track the smartphone market. On visibility Breen said there is 'significantly more visibility versus a year ago', highest for anything touching the data center: 'Most of the customers are talking about '27.'
quarterly_data.figure: CID approximately 12% of Q4 revenue, up approximately 29% sequentially and 32% year-over-year; FY2025 CID up 29%; satellite communications over $100 million; 2026 CID growth over 30%

quarterly_data.signal: GF delivered on its objective to roughly double silicon photonics revenue within the CID end market, to over $200 million in 2025. Even on this higher base it expects to NEARLY DOUBLE the silicon photonics contribution again in 2026, driven by strong customer demand, a robust ramp in supply capacity and the integration of Advanced Micro Foundry (AMF, Singapore), whose acquisition closed in November last year and is expected to be accretive to corporate gross margin targets in 2026. As pluggable applications ramp and co-packaged optics begins to scale, management now believes GF is on a path to a $1 billion run rate revenue level for silicon photonics by the end of 2028 - 'a substantial acceleration from our prior objective.' The majority of photonics revenue today is in the pluggable space, and silicon photonics comes through at a highly accretive gross margin.
quarterly_data.figure: silicon photonics revenue over $200 million in 2025; nearly double in 2026; $1 billion run rate revenue level by the end of 2028

quarterly_data.signal: In Q4 GF secured an important co-packaged optics design win for scale-up networks on its CLO silicon photonics platform, with photonic IC design wins at both endpoints of the scale-up network - 'an important step in the industry's rollout of CPO.' Breen said the CPO transition was always 'a '27 scale ramp more than a '26 scale ramp', and design wins and tape-out planning indicate it is on track because 'CPO is the only way to address certain performance workloads, especially on scale up networks'; the form-factor changes will drive significant increases of content. Technology roadmap: an offering for 200 gig per lane technologies today and a road map to 400 gig per lane and beyond; the InfiniLink design team in Cairo, Egypt helps customers building co-packaged optics solutions onboard faster; the collaboration with Corning brings detachable fiber attach, which management called critical for the transition to co-packaged optics; silicon photonics is being scaled in Singapore and the U.S., including on a 300-millimeter platform.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO design win for scale-up networks in Q4; CPO a '27 scale ramp; 200 gig per lane today, road map to 400 gig per lane

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and capex: FY2026 non-IFRS net capex is expected at 15% to 20% of full year revenue (versus 2025 net capex of approximately $574 million, or 8% of revenue), driven primarily by strong customer demand in capacity corridors where GF is OVERSUBSCRIBED - silicon photonics, FDX and SiGe - plus establishing new capabilities such as advanced packaging. Breen: 'those corridors are running hot'; GF is meeting customer demand today, but the ramp profiles of designs already won and now taping out require investment, done within the existing 4-wall footprint (New York, Burlington and a legacy facility being converted in Germany) with quick ramps, good capital efficiency and eligibility for government support. High-performance SiGe (TIAs and driver ICs) is pulled through by pluggable optical transceivers, and that capacity is being 'very, very well utilized' today. 2025 gross capex was up about 15% but net capex down about 7% as government support in the U.S., Germany and Singapore began to flow, expected to grow again in 2026. 2026 free cash flow margin is guided to approximately 10% of revenue as GF receives customer prepayments. Footprint: a $16 billion U.S. investment commitment (June 2025) to expand manufacturing and advanced packaging in New York and Vermont, and a EUR 1.1 billion Dresden expansion to over 1 million wafers per year by the end of 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 net CapEx 15% to 20% of full year revenue; 2025 net CapEx approximately $574 million (8% of revenue); 2026 free cash flow margin approximately 10%

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 guidance: revenue $1.625 billion, plus or minus $25 million; non-wafer revenue 10% to 12% of total (up from 8% to 12% in prior years, reflecting IP-related acquisitions); gross margin approximately 27%, plus or minus 100 basis points; operating expenses excluding share-based compensation $225 million plus or minus $10 million; operating margin 13.2%, plus or minus 180 basis points; diluted EPS $0.35, plus or minus $0.05; full-year effective tax rate in the high teens. Asked whether GF can exit 2026 at a 30% gross margin, Breen said 'I'm going to give you a yes for 2026 to the question of getting to our 30% target', with the long-term goal still the 40% gross margin target. Pricing: 'We definitely see a stronger pricing environment in 2026', with peers and GF's own customers raising prices; after deliberate 2025 smart-mobile price decisions no significant action is expected in 2026. Wafer volumes will grow in 2026, but mix is the main profitability driver.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 2026 revenue $1.625 billion, plus or minus $25 million; gross margin approximately 27%; operating margin 13.2%; EPS $0.35; a yes for 2026 to getting to our 30% target; 40% gross margin target long term

quarterly_data.signal: Design-win momentum and acquisitions: a record over 500 design wins in 2025, over 95% on a sole-source basis, with active engagements across all 4 U.S. hyperscalers, all 5 top automotive OEMs, all 6 mobile fabless and OEM and 7 of the top 8 industrial IDMs. New design wins driven specifically by GF's manufacturing footprint were worth well over $3 billion of combined expected lifetime revenue in 2025. Q4 wins included a 22 UX imaging design win with estimated lifetime revenue of over $500 million, and Broadcom selected GF's newly launched CBIC platform for a low-noise amplifier (the second major customer to adopt it). Among its 2025 customer announcements, GF expanded its long-standing Apple partnership to build wireless connectivity and power management chips in GF's U.S. fabs. Acquisitions: AMF is expected to deliver at least $75 million and MIPS $60 million to $100 million of revenue in 2026 (second-half skew), roughly $150 million across the two and roughly a point of incremental margin; InfiniLink is a design team supporting outer-year photonics and packaging revenue; the signed Synopsys ARC processor IP acquisition plus MIPS target a more than $1 billion incremental custom design and IP business over time.
quarterly_data.figure: over 500 design wins in 2025 (over 95% sole-source); footprint-driven wins well over $3 billion lifetime revenue; AMF at least $75 million and MIPS $60 million to $100 million in 2026
