players.product: ZeroFlap AECs, optical DSPs (Robin/Cardinal), SiPho PICs (Dust Photonics), retimers for AI clusters

connects_to.relationship: AEC (active electrical cable) supply — Credo's first AEC customer

contracts.signal: CEO Bill Brennan: 'Our first customer, Microsoft, the reason that they converted to AECs was really the functionality that we offered' — Credo developed a solution smart enough to sense when a TOR port was failing or about to fail and switch the data to a redundant TOR in a hitless manner; recounted as the origin of the AEC category whose playbook Credo is now applying to ZeroFlap Optics.

connects_to.relationship: ZeroFlap AEC supply — xAI defined the 7-meter AEC that covers every connection in the row of its liquid-cooled cluster

contracts.signal: CEO Bill Brennan named xAI as the customer that created the ZeroFlap concept: while building in another data center xAI was 'struggling mightily with link flaps' and could not keep cluster availability above even 90%. Moving into its own liquid-cooled data center, 'they came to us and said... What we want you to do is extend your AEC family from 3 meters to 7 meters because if you can do 7 meters, we can cover every connection in the row, and we can build a ZeroFlap cluster.' Brennan notes this is the ONLY transition where copper has replaced optical, for lengths up to 7 meters. He visited Memphis over the summer: xAI has achieved 99.9% uptime and can bring a cluster up in 5 days versus 6 to 8 weeks.
contracts.units: AEC family extended from 3 meters to 7 meters

connects_to.relationship: ZeroFlap Optics with real-time link telemetry for NIC-to-first-switch connections longer than 7 meters

contracts.signal: Oracle named as the customer behind the telemetry version of ZeroFlap: 'After we made this transition, Oracle came to us and said, Look, we'd love to address these problems as well, but our connections between the NIC and the first switch are longer than 7 meters, and we can't redesign. We've got what we've got.' Credo designed a custom DSP plus a software platform that lights up continuous real-time telemetry on each of the six links between a GPU and a switch (three in each direction), measuring eye height, SNR, post-FEC bit error rates and histograms to create a yellow 'check engine light' for a link instead of only green or red; it also identifies multipath interference caused by dust on the fiber plant and latent ESD damage, and mitigates likely link flaps by taking a link down in an orderly way rather than disrupting the cluster.

quarterly_data.signal: Hypergrowth on AI connectivity: FY2026 revenue $1.3B (+206% YoY, more than tripled) with non-GAAP net income up >5x to $662M; Q4 revenue a record $437M — MORE THAN ALL OF FY2025 — at 68.3% gross margin. AECs are the core engine: ZeroFlap active electrical cables deliver 'up to 1,000x greater reliability than commodity laser-based optical modules' at much lower power — now the preferred in-rack solution and used multi-rack up to 7 meters; strong hyperscaler + NeoCloud adoption at 100G/lane with 200G/lane emerging; PCIe Gen 6 AEC family on track. Thesis: AI infrastructure is 'increasingly constrained not by compute but by the reliability and efficiency of the connectivity fabric'.
quarterly_data.figure: FY26 rev $1.3B (+206%); ZeroFlap AEC ~1,000x reliability vs laser optics

quarterly_data.signal: FY2027 = optical INFLECTION: optical DSPs (Robin 100G/lane, Cardinal 200G/lane), SiPho PICs and ZeroFlap optics expected to EACH exceed $100M — total optical revenue >$600M in FY27, ramp accelerating in H2. Dust Photonics acquisition (closed late May 2026) adds differentiated silicon-photonics PIC technology spanning 800G/1.6T with a roadmap to 3.2T+ — its architecture needs SUBSTANTIALLY FEWER LASERS, easing industry supply constraints, and provides a direct path to CPO/NPO with initial revenue expected FY2028. Also: 200G/lane retimers supporting Ethernet + UALINK + eSUN; micro-LED active cables (AEC reliability at 30m optical reach) and OmniConnect 'Weaver' memory-IO gearbox both ramping FY2028.
quarterly_data.figure: FY27 optical >$600M total; Dust SiPho cuts laser count; CPO/NPO revenue FY28

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 FY2027 record: revenue $479 million, up 10% sequentially (above the high end of guidance) and up 115% year-over-year — the SEVENTH consecutive quarter of triple-digit year-over-year revenue growth, driven by substantial growth across four domestic customers. Non-GAAP gross margin 68% (midpoint of guide); non-GAAP operating expenses $95.2 million (+16% sequentially, above guide on strong R&D investment); non-GAAP operating income $230.6 million (operating margin 48.2%); non-GAAP net income a record $236.3 million (up 140% year-over-year per the CEO / more than doubled; +4% sequential vs $226.7 million in Q4), non-GAAP net margin 49.3%. Cash from operations $90.2 million (down $92.0 million sequentially on working capital); capex $7.3 million; free cash flow $82.9 million. Cash and equivalents $764.3 million, a decrease of $679 million primarily on the cash outlay for the DustPhotonics acquisition; inventory $313.1 million, up $62.2 million sequentially. Customer concentration: top four end customers each at or greater than 10% of revenue — 33%, 28%, 13% and 10% — with the top three the same as the prior quarter; three to four customers expected above 10% in coming quarters.
quarterly_data.figure: Rev $479M +10% QoQ / +115% YoY; non-GAAP GM 68%; non-GAAP net income record $236.3M; largest customer 33% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 FY2027 guide: revenue $525-535 million; non-GAAP gross margin 67-69%; non-GAAP operating expenses $100-105 million; diluted share count approximately 200 million (based on the current tariff regime, which remains fluid). Full-year FY2027: a second-half INFLECTION driven by more than $600 million of optical revenue — ZeroFlap Optics, silicon photonics PICs and optical DSPs EACH contributing more than $100 million — resulting in MORE THAN 85% year-over-year total revenue growth; non-GAAP gross margin broadly consistent with FY2026 levels; opex up approximately 55% year-over-year (well below revenue growth); non-GAAP net margin in the vicinity of 50%.
quarterly_data.figure: Q2 guide $525-535M; FY2027 more than 85% YoY growth; optical >$600M with ZeroFlap Optics, SiPho PICs and optical DSPs each >$100M

quarterly_data.signal: AECs remain Credo's largest business and continue to grow: DEEP RELATIONSHIPS WITH FIVE HYPERSCALERS and expanding NeoCloud engagement; AEC penetration increasing within existing customers as deployments scale, with the transition to 200G per lane / 1.6T ports ahead as the next growth vector. At 800G, copper AECs replaced laser-based optical transceivers for the GPU-to-first-switch connection on reliability and, secondarily, lower power. Management frames AECs as the 1m-7m segment of the pluggable transceiver market — with optical transceivers alone forecast to grow from 60 million units in 2026 to 175 million units by 2030 — and 1.6T AECs will deliver up to 6.5m reach, with some contribution in second-half fiscal 2027 and a much bigger ramp in fiscal 2028. AEC revenue more than doubled from 2024-2025 and more than tripled from 2025-2026; AECs keep growing, though slower than optics, which grows from a smaller base into a larger market.
quarterly_data.figure: Five hyperscaler AEC relationships; 1.6T AECs up to 6.5m reach — H2 FY2027 contribution, much bigger in fiscal 2028; transceiver market 60M to 175M units by 2030

quarterly_data.signal: Optical is the fastest-growing business, firmly on track for MORE THAN $600 million of FY2027 optical revenue. Optical DSPs: record Q1 revenue across 50G and 100G per lane deployments with a long tail for 800G ports; at 200G per lane, customer engagement with the 1.6T DSP is strong across both fully retimed and LRO solutions, and FIRST 1.6T DSP REVENUE remains on track for later this fiscal year. Silicon photonics: FIRST SiPho PIC revenue recognized in Q1 following the DustPhotonics acquisition, with initial wins in 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers expected to ramp throughout the year; the Dust team has secured DESIGN WINS WITH TWO MAJOR PLAYERS for next-generation ramps in FY2028 (possibly starting late this fiscal year) — the first two wins do NOT include the Credo DSP, leaving co-marketing upside. ZeroFlap Optics: production shipments underway, with additional customer ramps during fiscal 2027 across both 800G and 1.6T at both hyperscalers and neoclouds; the PILOT software platform provides continuous telemetry (real-time eye height, SNR, post-FEC histograms on all six links between XPU and switch, plus ESD-damage and fiber-dust detection) targeting cluster bring-up in five or six days versus six to eight weeks and driving to 99% uptime or higher — customers have cited link flaps costing greater than 10% or even approaching 20% of GPU utilization.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2027 optical >$600M; first 1.6T DSP revenue later this fiscal year; first SiPho PIC revenue in Q1; two major PIC design wins for FY2028 ramps

quarterly_data.signal: Scale-up optics push: Credo joined the Open Compute Project MSA consortium (open CPX) and sees increasing customer activity around NPO for scale-up networks, with CONFIRMED DESIGN WINS expected to begin ramping in fiscal 2028. Scale-up requires roughly 10x more density than scale-out pluggables — the industry conversation spans XPO, CPX, NPO and ultimately CPO — and Credo is approaching it agnostically: leading with the silicon photonics PIC in all NPO solutions including CPX, pursuing component sales where customers prefer them and complete optical engines / system-level solutions long term, bringing pluggable-ecosystem advantages (telemetry, interoperability, serviceability) to the consortium.
quarterly_data.figure: NPO scale-up design wins confirmed, ramping fiscal 2028; 10x density improvement needed vs scale-out

quarterly_data.signal: Retimers delivered record Q1 revenue, driven primarily by scale-up deployments of the Screaming Eagle retimer at 100G per lane, with the Blue Heron retimer beginning to contribute at 200G per lane; the Toucan retimer opportunity grows as PCIe Gen 6 adoption increases, and Screaming Eagle/Blue Heron span both Ethernet and UALink. Emerging growth engines with revenue beginning fiscal 2028: (1) Active LED Cables (ALCs) using microLED emitters — AEC-class reliability and power with reach of up to 30m; demonstrations planned at OFC in October; framed as a multi-billion-dollar pluggable-transceiver opportunity with a scale-up follow-on. (2) OmniConnect — a licensed low-power short-reach SerDes (reach up to 10in) plus Weaver gearboxes (LPDDR5 first, then LPDDR6, no XPU re-tape-out needed for the memory transition) attacking the memory fan-out limits of inference; potentially THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS of Credo content per GPU; first customer Positron's first announced product scales memory capacity up to 2TB (fitting frontier models fully in memory), and the roadmap targets bandwidth comparable to HBM5.
quarterly_data.figure: Record retimer revenue; ALCs up to 30m with OFC demos in October; OmniConnect thousands of dollars of content per GPU, revenue from fiscal 2028; Positron product up to 2TB memory

quarterly_data.signal: Supply readiness for the second-half optical ramp: Credo began leaning into its supply chain 18-24 months ago in anticipation of this direction; working capital is deliberately increasing (inventory $313.1 million, up $62.2 million sequentially) and management 'feels great' about the ability to supply increasing volumes in the second half and throughout the next couple of fiscal years — addressing analyst concerns about contract-manufacturer supply issues and rising prices in the foundry world.
quarterly_data.figure: Inventory $313.1M (+$62.2M QoQ) built ahead of the H2 optical ramp

quarterly_data.signal: Micro-emitter ALCs - reach, form factor and production date. Credo has been working on micro-emitter technology for three years because, at a core technology level, 'wide and slow' micro-emitters keep copper-like bulletproof reliability with much better power efficiency than laser-based optics. The technology reaches 30 meters, extending Credo from a 7-meter AEC reach to 30 meters 'with an equal level of reliability and power efficiency,' and the cable is 75% SMALLER BY TOTAL VOLUME than today's bulky 7-meter AECs at 200G per lane. Credo will demonstrate at OCP next month, then 'expect to go through qualification and then be IN PRODUCTION AT FY 2028.' Every ALC goes through the same qualification rigor as AECs - Credo runs live traffic through customers' own switches and NICs over every corner, deliberately breaking the link and strengthening it through firmware, so the customer only has to plug it in.

quarterly_data.signal: AECs grew again, driven by existing customers and new wins INCLUDING A FIFTH HYPERSCALER, with demand accelerating at hyperscalers and emerging Neocloud providers. Brennan: AECs are now the de facto standard for intra-rack and rack-to-rack connectivity up to 7 meters, increasingly displacing laser-based optical modules; ZeroFlap AECs deliver up to 1,000x better reliability than commodity laser-based optics at roughly half the power. Large-scale deployments run at 100 gig per lane with a long tail; 1.6-terabit AECs will support Ethernet, UALink and ESUN, and PCIe Gen6 AECs are sampling now for mass production in first half fiscal '27. At 200 gig per lane the value proposition is stronger with an ASP uplift, though reach shrinks 'from 7 meters to 5 meters'. Credo's strength is scale-out (with front end coming along; a couple of customers deploying in switch racks / disaggregated chassis); front end is expected to be 20% to 25% of the scale-out market. Brennan on 200G: 'NVIDIA is going to lead the charge with Vera Rubin, but many other customers will follow on a slower time line', and that market will be addressed by AECs plus laser-based modules, with ALCs ramping in.

ZF Optics adds continuous link-flap telemetry and autonomous mitigation via the Pilot software with switch-level SDK integration - the first time an optical transceiver has been taken up the stack to deliver real-time telemetry - and lets Credo address optical connectivity at any length inside the data center.

quarterly_data.signal: CPO / ELSFP EXTERNAL LASER SOURCE ECONOMICS: ELSFP (external light source for co-packaged optics) is in very limited production now, ramping later in 2026 and through 2027 to ~400,000 PIECES PER MONTH IN 2028. Laser power scaling is the constraint: CPO/ELSFP uses a 300mW laser vs 70mW in an 800G transceiver and 100mW in a 1.6T transceiver, with die size ~6x larger, so meeting CPO demand requires the industry laser market to be 8-10x BIGGER than today; the next generation of ELSFP moves to DWDM, where yield loss is 40-50% worse than 1310nm. Laser capacity carries a 21-24 MONTH equipment-to-high-volume lead time. AOI is engaged with ~5 CPO customers on 3-4 year demand; several have already qualified AOI on fixed-wavelength CPO laser / ELSFP, with DWDM the current focus. High-volume ELSFP manufacturing is 'more like late Q3 next year' (late 2027). Houston laser fab capacity to grow ~300% by Q3 2027 plus a SECOND FAB cleanroom ~4x the size of the current facility (adding MOCVD, epi, steppers). Margin mix: laser gross margin 55-65%, ELSFP module ('EOSAP') >50%, both landing H2 2027. AOI is absent from first-generation CPO deployments purely because laser capacity must first feed AOI's own transceivers.
quarterly_data.figure: ELSFP ~400k pcs/month in 2028; 300mW CPO laser vs 70mW(800G)/100mW(1.6T); industry laser capacity needs 8-10x; laser GM 55-65%

quarterly_data.signal: BOTTLENECK HAS MOVED FROM LASERS TO DSP/TIA: because AOI makes its own lasers in-house it avoids the laser shortage that management calls 'the biggest bottleneck right now for the transceiver business' and 'the number one issue' for competitors; AOI's binding constraints for 800G/1.6T are instead DSP and TIA supply, where 'the whole supply chain is very tight' for 1.6T - AOI says its supplier ranks it FOURTH priority under a long-term partnership, with calls once or twice a week. INDIUM PHOSPHIDE SUBSTRATE: supply secured into end-2027 and 'incrementally better' than last quarter - not currently a limiter; AOI has just moved to 4-INCH substrate volume manufacturing and buys from 2 European + 2 Japanese + 3 Chinese suppliers, and is negotiating partnerships or a possible JOINT VENTURE with 2-3 of them for 2028-2029 volumes (laser capacity growing 'much more than a factor of 10'). Proprietary in-house production machinery insulates AOI from the industry's equipment-delivery bottlenecks.

Critically, MACOM says it will NOT build or supply optical engines - in Data Center it is a chip supplier, not a multichip assembly or module supplier. It describes the architectural evolution as pluggable transceivers with DSPs, to LPO platforms that remove the DSP, morphing into smaller package-less NPO platforms; those architectures still need drivers and TIAs, but with much higher density - smaller parts, more channels, lower power, and varied form factors using wire bonds, bumped devices or flip chip, plus through-silicon-via options. The 75-MILLIWATT CW LASER qualification continues: MACOM is well into HTOL testing (typically 5,000 hours) with data described as exceptional, is gaining confidence but cannot yet declare success, and is developing plans for a POTENTIAL START TO PRODUCTION IN LATE CALENDAR 2027, scoping modest capex and fab space for a rapid high-volume ramp for a few strategic customers. CEO Steve Daly called bringing a CW laser into production in 2028 'a watershed moment' that could be a very large revenue contributor. Separately, demand for MACOM's 25G DFB lasers (100G QSFP, CWDM4, LR4) is rising with urgency because of a GENERAL SUPPLY SHORTAGE OF INDIUM PHOSPHIDE DFB LASERS. MACOM expects to gain meaningful indium phosphide market share over the next three years; its Ann Arbor, Michigan facility has built photodiodes for over a decade and grows its own epitaxy by MBE.

If hyperscalers have to shift share between transceiver companies because of new regulations, 'we would expect to follow that business to those other manufacturers' - a customer mix shift rather than a demand loss, since MACOM has relationships with most transceiver companies in the industry. MACOM has NO MANUFACTURING IN CHINA, only about 85 employees there in application sales and logistics supporting Scandinavian telecom design centres and the optical industry, and the vast majority of what it sells into China is exported back out inside systems typically headed to the U.S.

quarterly_data.signal: MACOM published its 2026-2030 Growth Strategy Plan to the Board in mid-July and reset its served addressable market to approximately $15 BILLION IN 2027 - roughly $6 billion Industrial and Defense, $6 billion Data Center and about $3 billion Telecom - up about 20% to 30% from 2026. Named accelerators for the next three to five years: more 200-gig-per-lane PAM4 products, added indium phosphide capacity, new scale-up, scale-out and scale-across programs, NPO growing significantly from 2028, coherent light opportunities, PCIe 6, and linear equalizers. On equalizers specifically, MACOM sees opportunity in both active copper cables and on-board (PCB) use, and said ONE LARGE HYPERSCALER is looking to deploy that type of cable solution at large volumes, where MACOM would expect to participate when it moves to production. R&D spending has roughly doubled in three years, from about $132 million in 2023 to almost $250 million this year.

LEO satellite broadband and direct-to-device remain robust: MACOM serves four or five major LEO customers, has two or three major LEO programs starting production at the end of this calendar year and the beginning of next, and this quarter WAS SELECTED TO SUPPORT A NEXT-GENERATION SATELLITE OPTICAL COMMUNICATION PLATFORM at a large satellite OEM - a win management expects to drive growth for two to three years, won because all the critical ICs for the system could be sourced from MACOM. The commercial RF power team traditionally aimed at 5G base stations is now also targeting LEO, since 5G technology applies directly to LEO D2D. Within Telecom, 5G is still the largest piece with two competitors having exited in the last three to four years; cable infrastructure is growing around 40% year over year and metro long-haul over 50% this year.

quarterly_data.signal: MACOM raised its fiscal 2026 Data Center year-over-year revenue growth base case from 20% to 35 to 40%, with upside that is 'a bit unquantifiable right now'. CEO Stephen Daly said 'the key underlying driver is 1.6T', where MACOM sees the most design wins transitioning into production runs; the Data Center backlog is very healthy and the second half should be stronger than the first half in absolute revenue dollars. Growth is primarily in pluggable optical modules and optical cables using its 800G and 1.6T PAM4 products (supporting DSP, LPO and LRO module architectures, plus coherent DCI including ZR and ZR Lite), and hyperscaler capital investments are robust. A significant portion of Data Center revenue is 400 gig and above with 1.6T the fastest-growing portion; 'The real action is at 200 gig per lane PAM4' and next-generation coherent, while 25 gig per lane NRZ is holding up, 50 gig per lane PAM4 is flat and 100 gig per lane PAM4 is solid. MACOM supports all of the US hyperscalers as well as international hyperscalers, selling to builders of modules, AOCs and cables. Management does not frame the growth as share gain: 'I think the market's growing. We're winning designs.' The product roadmap extends to 3.2T.
quarterly_data.figure: Data Center FY2026 growth base case raised from 20% to 35 to 40%

quarterly_data.signal: LPO, LRO and copper: MACOM now has three hyperscalers embracing LPO and is 'in various phases of production' with them - in all cases 100 gig per lane for generally 800 gig modules; management expects LPO to remain a small part of the market for the next one to two years and to evolve into NPO/CPO/XPO. Customers are also investigating LRO at 1.6T using 200 gig per lane chips, and management sees LRO as more likely to happen first than 1.6T LPO. LPO interest is also appearing in PCIe, NPO and telecom front haul. On copper, there is renewed interest in MACOM's linear equalizers to extend active copper cable (ACC) reach at 800G and 1.6T and for backplanes (eliminating retimers, and important at 400 gig per lane), but Q1 contained no ACC revenue; management sees the ACC opportunity as bigger than backplane equalizers, and some customers are evaluating converting AECs to ACCs. MACOM launched a PCIe 6 optical chipset supporting sideband data streams over fiber and a new PCIe 7 equalizer, giving it new exposure to the compute side of the data center network.
quarterly_data.figure: three hyperscalers in LPO production phases (100 gig per lane, 800 gig modules); no ACC revenue in Q1

quarterly_data.signal: Photonics and CPO/NPO: demand for MACOM's 200 gig per lane photodetectors (for 800G and 1.6T) continues to grow, with indications that demand will remain strong into calendar 2027; the indium phosphide photodetector business is growing rapidly, higher-speed photodetectors are in development, and EML lasers are in test. CW lasers: two customers - module makers, the first line of entry before a hyperscaler PCN process adds MACOM to the approved vendor list - have confirmed MACOM's 75-milliwatt CW lasers meet their requirements electrically for their silicon photonics solutions, followed by a qualification phase lasting 'some number of months' and a fab production-readiness review. CEO Stephen Daly called it 'a watershed moment because six months ago, we were not in a position where we had a compliant laser'; MACOM does not make 400-milliwatt class lasers and does not sell lasers into 1.6 applications today, so this would be share gain. The product set sold into CPO or NPO platforms is very similar to pluggables (drivers, TIAs, photodetectors and possibly lasers); these platforms are moving quickly to silicon photonics, putting heavy demand on CW laser and photodetector chips, with far more channels per chip, and some systems are moving to coherent light. MACOM's future products are increasingly optimized for CPO and NPO.
quarterly_data.figure: 75-milliwatt CW lasers: two customers confirmed requirements met electrically; 200 gig per lane photodetector demand strong into calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and supply: MACOM is adding indium phosphide photodetector manufacturing capacity to keep up with customers' forecasted demand (amount not disclosed for competitive reasons). The North Carolina (RTP) fab has 'a very aggressive plan to increase output by 30%', with some equipment bought and cycle-time reduction as the site's number one priority. Gross margin gains this year and next come mainly from higher utilization of the Massachusetts fab and to some degree the French fab, whose three-inch to six-inch wafer transition is targeted to be fully qualified and released to production by June 2026; one high-mix fab runs GaAs, GaN, silicon and indium phosphide. Benefits from insourcing IPDs and capacitors now bought from a third-party vendor will most likely come in 2027 and beyond. On supply, 'we are absolutely in ramp mode in various programs', and availability of indium phosphide and other exotic materials is a key focus; pricing is rational, and 'we're in an environment where there is scarcity in some areas'. Fiscal 2026 capex is still estimated at $50 million to $55 million (Q1 capex $12.9 million).

quarterly_data.signal: Telecom: MACOM's previously announced $55 million satellite contract (with the potential of an additional $25 million add-on) is planned to start production in 2026, delayed mainly by satellite system changes flowed down from the customer, which management views as positive because added functionality should bring new customers to the constellation. MACOM says it is engaged at some level with all of the major LEO constellations (microwave, optics, satellite-to-satellite, direct-to-device and ground stations), has multiple SATCOM LEO programs in design, and expects SATCOM to grow nicely into 2027. In 5G, one competitor is exiting the RF power GaN market; MACOM hired a team of experienced engineers and is sampling next-generation GaN4 products, but expects share gains to take one or two years with a flat RAN market in 2026. Cable TV is expected to be a modest contributor to fiscal 2026 telecom growth.

'The downside risk is tiny and the upside opportunity is immense', with the real downside being that if the capacity is not put in place customers have to go somewhere else. quarterly_data.signal: Datacom diversification status: Fabrinet is actually shipping to both hyperscale-direct and merchant transceiver manufacturers right now, and it is early days. The non-NVIDIA datacom customers are mostly initially 800 gig short reach transceivers and then moving to 1.6 in the future, with the initial foray at 800 gig. Grady reiterated Fabrinet will never become an ODM or own the IP - companies like Ciena, Cisco and Nokia would be deeply upset if it became a product company - and said Fabrinet has been picking up and winning business with some customers precisely because some competitors chose the ODM route. Management said it does not overly analyse share (customers do not always disclose it) and focuses instead on growing each opportunity to the multi-$100 million level where it can properly resource the customer. Beyond hyperscale, Fabrinet is also working with quantum compute customers that would fall into the new data center category, because moving those workloads around will need optics and not just electronics.

quarterly_data.signal: First margin math on NPO/CPO: on a typical product, if COGS is 100%, roughly 70%-80% is material and 20% is value add. For NPO the material content is much lower - in many cases the wafer is consigned by the customer and Fabrinet singulates it, does the packaging and the testing at die and device level - so it is much higher value add, probably a lower ASP but a higher margin, and Grady said NPO 'would be much better gross margin than our traditional business'. He cautioned the business needs a mix of both higher-volume lower-margin work and this higher-margin lower-ASP work, and described NPO as probably a little bit more straightforward than CPO, with the opportunity in NPO extending well beyond ELSFPs to the packaging of the devices themselves.

quarterly_data.signal: OCS ramp timing put on the clock for the first time: Fabrinet has shipped some OCS product but it is quite small today, and is working with a number of companies, one of whom it is actually shipping product to, while the others are early days and more startup-type companies. ORDERS $10.7 BILLION — a BOOK-TO-BILL OF 1.23:1, implying demand running well ahead of even 55% sales growth. Adjusted diluted EPS $1.35 versus $0.81 a year ago (+67%). Q3 2026 GUIDANCE STEPS UP AGAIN: sales $9.3-9.4B, representing 50-52% growth, with adjusted EPS $1.40-1.42 (+51-53%) — and the guide excludes future acquisitions. Two companies acquired during the quarter; $515M returned to shareholders ($208M buybacks + $307M dividends).

CALL — IT DATACOM IS NOW 43% OF THE COMPANY AND IT'S ALL AI: IT-datacom sales rose 89% in USD and 63% ORGANICALLY (+22% sequentially) with 'virtually all of this growth driven by sales of AI-RELATED PRODUCTS'; Q3 guided to a FURTHER mid-teens sequential increase; an analyst framed Amphenol's AI revenue RUN RATE at $10.5-11 BILLION without dispute. The reason for all of this, of course, is because timing needs to get closer, timing needs to get more clean, the signal needs to be less attenuated, and just like in power, you have VPD, vertical delivery, we think there's a concept called VTD, which is getting closer and closer to the chip, either below, embedded in the substrate or above. I think that this could start as early as 2028, maybe 2029.' He called it 'mostly incremental' rather than cannibalistic because it lands at the very high end.
quarterly_data.figure: a billion to 1.5 billion more of SAM; could start as early as 2028, maybe 2029

Vashist: 'It's had a tremendous clock growth, and that growth, I think, continues... I think it's also fair to say that next year is probably very similar to that growth rate of well above 50%, maybe in the 60%, 70%, even 80% range for that TPD business. That is, by the way, without that much help from SiTime.' Cross-selling is already opening doors: TPD 'dragged us into very large organizations where we didn't have much penetration in the hyperscalers, one of the large hyperscalers', and SiTime is taking TPD into chip companies it had not penetrated. On renewal: 'I fully expect that as our 2027 10-year deal with them sort of comes off, there will be another one that will extend the time.'

quarterly_data.signal: MIL-AERO COULD REACH $100 MILLION: CEO Rajesh Vashist said the automotive, industrial, military, aero and defense business 'grew last quarter at more than 50% growth rate' and 'we think that the military aero business alone could be $100 million shortly, followed quickly by the auto business'. A new push into smart grids adds 'incremental SAM of a couple hundred million'. Asked whether, in the medium term, aero and defense would 'grow above the rate of-' (question cut off), he answered 'Absolutely.'
quarterly_data.figure: military aero business alone could be $100 million shortly; smart grids incremental SAM of a couple hundred million

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 revenue was $113.6 million, up 88% year-over-year and essentially flat with Q4, which CFO Beth Howe called significantly better than anticipated at the start of the quarter, driven by stronger than expected AI data center demand; non-GAAP gross margin 64.5% (up 7.1 percentage points, about half from mix, half from cost and absorption), operating margin 28% versus 3% a year ago, EPS $1.44 versus $0.26.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $113.6 million, up 88% YoY; gross margin 64.5%; operating margin 28%; EPS $1.44

quarterly_data.signal: Communications, Enterprise and Data Center (CED) revenue was $75.7 million, 66.6% of total revenue, up 158% year-over-year and 17% sequentially; CEO Rajesh Vashist called it the 8th consecutive quarter of triple-digit percentage growth and said the high growth trend continues. Demand spans AI infrastructure 'including optical modules, switches, SmartNICs, and accelerator platforms'; book-to-bill is growing with pull-through from the channel, keeping inventories at target.
quarterly_data.figure: CED revenue $75.7 million (66.6% of revenue), +158% YoY, +17% QoQ

quarterly_data.signal: Guidance (SiTime standalone, no Renesas timing business, which had not yet closed): full-year revenue growth raised to at least 80%, well above the prior expectation and the 25%-30% long-term target, reflecting the depth of the order book and customers' confidence in their own demand forecasts, particularly in CED. June quarter revenue $140 million-$150 million, up more than 100% year-over-year; gross margin approximately 65% ±1 point; opex $46 million-$47 million; non-GAAP EPS $1.85-$2.00. Beth Howe expects consumer to be a larger share of mix in the back half, which may modulate gross margin, but still above that 60% level.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue growth at least 80%; Q2 revenue $140 million-$150 million (up more than 100% YoY); gross margin approximately 65% ±1 point; EPS $1.85-$2.00

quarterly_data.signal: Inference drives timing content: Vashist said inference infrastructure built on newer XPU 'needs 2 to 4 times more timing content per system than in training infrastructure'; GPU utilization in inference is 20% to 40% and targeted to reach 50% to 60%, with time synchronization critical to that, driving demand for high-ASP, high-margin Elite and Elite RF Super-TCXOs. The new Elite 2 Super-TCXO family delivers up to 3 times better synchronization than Elite; this product class addresses $1.5 billion of cumulative SAM over the next five years. When an analyst called it both an ASP and a unit driver, Vashist agreed ('That's right').
quarterly_data.figure: 2 to 4 times more timing content per inference system vs training; Elite 2 up to 3 times better synchronization; $1.5 billion cumulative SAM over the next five years

quarterly_data.signal: Optical generation shift: SiTime expects meaningful adoption of 1.6 terabit optical modules in 2026, with higher frequencies and resilience needs driving demand for its advanced oscillators at a higher price than those used in 800G, while oscillators for 400G and 800G keep shipping strongly for at least the next two years. Vashist said 1.6T is 'growing, as we said the last time, at a higher rate than we had anticipated last year', and connectivity demand includes AEC active cabling. On co-packaged optics, customer discussions show 'even greater strength', e.g. CPO switches, where timing content can be up to 3 times higher.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO switch timing content up to 3 times higher; 400G/800G oscillator shipments strong for at least the next two years

quarterly_data.signal: Customer breadth and share: Vashist said SiTime sells to GPUs, XPUs, TPUs, into AI switches, and in connectivity to 'more than 15-20 module makers'; growth now includes penetrating customers where it was previously under-penetrated plus share expansion, higher ASPs and volumes. In the module business, where volumes 'have soared recently', some competitors using older technologies 'have been unable to keep up'. SiTime sells at a premium and still shares module business with quartz oscillator suppliers, noting there are credible suppliers even at 1.6T. Its clock portfolio of around 50 clocks is gaining traction.
quarterly_data.figure: more than 15-20 module makers; around 50 clocks

quarterly_data.signal: Supply position: Vashist said capacity is 'very solid' - MEMS chips come from Bosch and analog chips on older geometries (180 nanometers, 150, 130 nanometers) come mostly from TSMC, all in good shape; there are occasional back-end challenges with OSATs because of volume, but nothing beyond usual execution issues. Changes made in early 2025 (and maybe even late 2024) around back-end automation and AI in test programs and characterization raised productivity with less CapEx. 'We see no issues around supply chain in particular.'
quarterly_data.figure: analog chips at 180 nanometers, 150, 130 nanometers mostly from TSMC

quarterly_data.signal: Market sizing and model: SiTime addresses a $4 billion SAM within an $11 billion timing total available market. Against a long-term model of 25%-30% annual revenue growth (significantly exceeded), and targets of 65% gross margin and 30% operating margin, management expected to reach those margin targets in Q2 2026. The Renesas timing acquisition remained on track pre-close, bringing about 150 odd people, mostly engineers, with planned CapEx for new equipment in that business and no cost-structure surprises.
quarterly_data.figure: $4 billion SAM in $11 billion timing TAM; targets 65% gross margin and 30% operating margin expected in Q2 2026

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 revenue was $113.3 million, up 66% year over year and 36% sequentially - the first quarter above $100 million - and significantly higher than expected as customer demand kept strengthening; gross margin was 61.2% (up 240 basis points year over year, exiting 2025 above 60% as promised) on a mix shift toward higher-margin products; operating margin 30%; non-GAAP EPS $1.53 versus $0.48 a year ago. Full-year 2025 revenue was $326.7 million, up 61%, with gross margin 59.3% and non-GAAP EPS $3.20; every end-customer segment and every region grew.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue $113.3 million, up 66% YoY and 36% QoQ; gross margin 61.2%; operating margins of 30%; EPS $1.53; FY2025 revenue $326.7 million, up 61%

quarterly_data.signal: Communications, Enterprise and Data Center (CED) contributed $64.6 million, or 57% of total revenue, up 160% year over year - the seventh consecutive quarter of over 100% year-over-year growth - with broad-based growth from multiple customers across AI and data centers. Management said CED was just 12% of revenue at IPO, after which SiTime created a strategic plan to expand it to 40 to 50%, and it makes up 53% of revenue today; the 2026 CED forecast has grown since the November call, driven by increases in AI CapEx spending.
quarterly_data.figure: CED revenue $64.6 million (57% of revenue), up 160% YoY

quarterly_data.signal: Demand remained very strong exiting 2025: SiTime disclosed (though it does not usually discuss it) that book-to-bill was over 1.5 at the end of Q4, with 'excellent visibility for the year'. Most bookings come from CED, with customers booking through 2026; CFO Beth Howe said the backlog is typically well within twelve months, definitely weighted to Q1 and Q2, with some customers already booking meaningfully into the second half. Distributor and contract-manufacturer inventory ended in line with target on strong sell-through.
quarterly_data.figure: book to bill was over 1.5; backlog well within twelve months, weighted to Q1 and Q2

quarterly_data.signal: 1.6T transition: the two to four times increase in computing power of new XPUs, GPUs and CPUs is driving faster networking and accelerating adoption of 1.6 terabit optical modules; customers raised their 2026 forecast for SiTime oscillators used in 1.6T modules by 50%, over and above the increase reported in November. 1.6T needs higher clocking frequencies, which carry higher ASPs - CEO Rajesh Vashist put it 'in the tens of percent up in ASP' - and unit deployments are 'far more than we had thought on our last call in November'. Demand for oscillators in 800 gigabit modules remains strong. SiTime is designed in at a large number of optical module suppliers, in AEC active cables and in retimers; Vashist said those optical, smart-cable and retimer sockets use oscillators, not clocks.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 forecast for 1.6T module oscillators up 50%; ASP up in the tens of percent

quarterly_data.signal: Compute side: hyperscalers are deploying more XPUs for training and getting ready for inference, which since November has driven a 50% increase in the 2026 forecast for SiTime's Super TCXOs, used in both computing infrastructure and the supporting smart NICs (network interface cards). Vashist: 'You see Google spending. You see Meta spending. There is no stopping in the AI data center world.' SiTime grew 40% in 2024 and north of 60% in 2025 and he expects a series of growth years from AI, including beyond data centers. He sized the whole timing market at $10 billion to $11 billion, growing 5% to 6% a year, probably $17 billion to $18 billion in ten years.
quarterly_data.figure: Super TCXO 2026 forecast up 50%

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 guidance (Renesas timing business excluded, as it was not expected to close in Q1): revenue $101 to $104 million, up roughly 70% year over year at the midpoint, with first-quarter seasonality below the historical average and CED growing sequentially while consumer declines seasonally; gross margin approximately 62% plus or minus half a point on the richer CED mix; operating expenses $39 million to $40 million; interest income approximately $7 million; non-GAAP EPS $1.10 to $1.17. The CFO expects the CED-versus-consumer mix to be the biggest gross-margin driver through 2026, with revenue growing faster than operating expenses.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 revenue $101 to $104 million (up roughly 70% YoY at the midpoint); gross margin approximately 62%; EPS $1.10 to $1.17

quarterly_data.signal: Announced the acquisition of Renesas' timing business (the Timing Products Division, ICS then IDT heritage; 500 clock products and 160 engineers) for $1.5 billion in cash plus approximately 4.13 million newly issued SiTime shares (15% symmetrical collar). The cash portion is funded from cash on hand and approximately $900 million of committed debt financing from Wells Fargo; leverage is targeted under two times within twenty-four months of closing, closing is expected by the end of 2026, and China SAMR approval is not expected to be needed. The business is expected to add $300 million of revenue in the twelve months after close at approximately 70% gross margins, 75% from CED, and SiTime's pro forma 2025 CED revenue almost doubles with Renesas' AI data center comms revenue. Management said the deal is accretive to non-GAAP EPS in the first full year, keeps the 25% to 30% long-term growth target intact (clocking grows more slowly than oscillators), moves SiTime faster to the upper end of its 60% to 65% gross-margin target with operating margins above 30%, and accelerates the path to $1 billion in revenue.
quarterly_data.figure: $1.5 billion in cash and approximately 4.13 million newly issued shares; $900 million committed debt; $300 million revenue in the twelve months after close at approximately 70% gross margins; 75% CED

quarterly_data.signal: Cross-sell from the Renesas timing deal: Renesas clocks are typically designed in alongside quartz crystal, opening those sockets to SiTime's MEMS oscillators, while SiTime already has design wins in AI GPUs, accelerator cards and switches where the clock is Renesas' or another competitor's, allowing an oscillator-plus-clock offer that is 'notionally integrated' with one source of supply. The deal brings faster access to 10 hyperscalers, seven AI server leaders, 10 networking and communication vendors, plus leading automotive OEMs and tier ones; customer overlap is reasonably solid but product overlap minimal. A separate MOU explores integrating SiTime's Titan resonators into Renesas microcontrollers (a several-billion-dollar MCU revenue base), and the Renesas CEO joins SiTime's board at closing.
quarterly_data.figure: 10 hyperscalers, seven AI server leaders, 10 networking and communication vendors

quarterly_data.signal: Supply chain: Vashist said the acquired timing business is fabless IDT heritage - 'they are TSMC point one eight micron, which is fantastic. Since TSMC is already a great supplier to SiTime Corporation' - and also uses GlobalFoundries at 55 nanometer, with back-end partners in Asia; its engineers sit mainly in Ottawa, South San Jose and Tempe, Arizona, plus Shanghai. SiTime had supply challenges early in 2025 while launching new products into surging demand, but 'more than caught up in Q3, Q4'; the CFO said SiTime is working closely with supply-chain partners to secure the supply and lines it needs and to watch costs amid 'the tightening that I think everybody is seeing'.
quarterly_data.figure: GlobalFoundries in the 55 nanometer and TSMC point one eight micron (acquired timing business)

quarterly_data.signal: Beyond the data center, autonomous systems and physical AI are lifting automotive, industrial and aerospace/defense: management cited up to $20 of precision timing content in humanoid robots and up to $15 in level four ADAS robotaxis, and expects each of the automotive, defense and industrial businesses to exceed $100 million annually in the next few years. Q4 automotive, industrial and aerospace revenue was $24.5 million (22% of revenue, up 19%); consumer, IoT and mobile was $24.2 million (21%, up 7%), with the largest consumer customer contributing $17 million and a consumer design win expected to ramp meaningfully through 2026.

quarterly_data.signal: FIRST $3 BILLION QUARTER: Q2 revenue $3.036B, up 37.7% YoY and 12.1% sequentially; non-GAAP EPS $1.02 (+39.7%); non-GAAP operating margin 49.9% (GAAP 45.4%). Q3 2026 guide: revenue approximately $3.3 BILLION with non-GAAP operating margin 48-49%. Deferred revenue swelled to $5.10B current + $1.77B non-current = ~$6.87B total (from ~$5.37B) — a forward-demand signal. CEO Jayshree Ullal: 'Customers see networking as the CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM for infrastructure from the client to campus to data and AI centers.' NEW PRODUCTS: introduced 1.6 Tbps AI FABRIC PLATFORMS (7060XE7 Series) INCLUDING LIQUID-COOLED OPTIONS optimized for scale-up, scale-out and scale-across networks; new Etherlink platforms deliver up to 100 Tbps of system bandwidth and support LINEAR PLUGGABLE OPTICS, cutting interconnect power ~60% versus traditional pluggables; plus MRC protocol and SRv6 innovations aimed at maximizing AI cluster utilization and resilience.
quarterly_data.figure: First $3B+ quarter ($3.036B, +37.7%); Q3 guide ~$3.3B; 1.6T liquid-cooled AI fabric (7060XE7); LPO -60% power

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — GUIDE RAISED A THIRD TIME; SUPPLY CHAIN REBUILT: FY2026 revenue raised to ~$12.6B = 40% GROWTH (+$2.1B vs the $10.5B Analyst Day plan, +$1.1B vs May's $11.5B) — the raise deliberately UNALLOCATED across AI fabrics (goal >=$3.5B), campus (>=$1.25B), core front-end data center ('isn't going to be flat' — enterprise, new logos, international) and routing; operating margin RAISED to 48-49% (Q2 hit 49.9%). Supply chain: Jayshree — 'the INDUSTRY is going to have a TWO-YEAR problem... I don't think we get out of it as an industry TILL 2028,' but Arista's specific H1 actions pay off in H2: MULTI-YEAR PURCHASE COMMITMENTS NEARLY TRIPLED YoY to $9.7 BILLION (from $3.6B; $8.9B in Q1); MEMORY SUPPLY SECURED FOR 2026 with visibility WELL INTO 2027 (DDR4/DDR5/NAND); PCB + optics capacity buildable in a 12-month window; a NEW LIQUID-COOLING SUPPLY CHAIN stood up (cold plates, quick disconnects, tubing with capacity agreements); 3 CMs + 3 distribution hubs (US/Asia/Mexico). Guidance is explicitly supply-gated: 'guiding based on what we're CONFIDENT we can get the supply for — if supply released more, there is opportunity to do better.' Price increases only help 'end of the year or more like next year' (backlog); FY GM held 62-64% including memory/silicon cost inflation. Etherlink AI-fabric customers now EXCEED 100 CUMULATIVE (from 4-5 in 2024).
quarterly_data.figure: FY26 raised to ~$12.6B (+40%, 3rd raise); purchase commitments ~3x YoY to $9.7B; memory secured into 2027; liquid-cooling chain built; >100 AI customers

quarterly_data.signal: CALL — OPEN CPO STANCE AND THE SCALE-UP VIEW: scale-up philosophy = 'COPPER IF YOU CAN, OPTICS IF YOU MUST.' Arista rejects the ~5 proprietary CPO implementations circulating and is committing to ONE OPEN CPO — socketed optical engines, pigtail fibers, fully pre-tested modules, a truly open multi-vendor interface (often called NPO) — with trials/examples NEXT YEAR; 'the MAJORITY of the world will still remain PLUGGABLE OPTICS AND COPPER; there will be SOME co-packaged optics in 2028 and 2029.' Scale-up positioning: 'we live in an NVIDIA world' — where NVIDIA supplies the full NVLink vertical stack there is little Arista participation (Arista wins scale-out/across), but for NON-NVIDIA accelerators (AMD MI series, Google TPUs — 'increasingly a FORMIDABLE training processor', in-house XPUs, inference chips) Arista works BOTH scale-up and scale-out, including CUSTOM RACKS tuned to customers' engines; 'feels like InfiniBand 2-3 years ago... it will take time to move from proprietary NVLink to alternatives, even if Ethernet's really good — I expect us to do much better there.' 1.6T cadence (history repeats 800G's trials-2023/24 -> ramp-2025/26): TRIALS H2 2026 with single-digit VERY LARGE customers; REAL PRODUCTION 2027 (liquid-cooling infrastructure required). EOS innovations for AI fabrics: SSU hitless upgrades, MRC packet-spray/reassembly (kills hash-collision slowdowns), SRv6 explicit-path load balancing with real-time congestion signals — one binary from scale-out to scale-across.
quarterly_data.figure: Open CPO (socketed/NPO) trials 2027; majority stays pluggable+copper, some CPO 2028-29; non-NVIDIA scale-up = the opening (InfiniBand analogy); 1.6T production 2027

quarterly_data.signal: PURCHASE COMMITMENT TRAJECTORY AND WHERE THE TIGHTNESS SITS: CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said purchase commitments were about $3.6 billion three quarters ago and $9.6 billion at the end of Q2 - basically tripling - and that this balance is already covering the second half of next year, since chips carry a year lead time going into Q3 next year. The structural pressure is at the top of fab capacity; Arista found vendor arrangements on fab capacity and memory that it says sorted 2026 and 2027, but peripheral parts (PCBs, capacitors) remain Whac-A-Mole and 'I don't think anyone's out of the woods when it comes to the full supply chain for networking data centers generally'.
quarterly_data.figure: about $3.6 billion; $9.6 billion at the end of Q2; a year lead time for chips going into Q3 next year

quarterly_data.signal: XPO / NPO / CPO ROADMAP WITH DATES: SVP Cloud and AI Networking Tyson Lamoreaux said 'XPO early deployments second half of next year, really ramping in 2028, and probably 12 months behind that is where we start to see some of that CPO ramp occur'. The sequence is copper as long as possible, then NPO/XPO (XPO is the NPO-based architecture) for the multi-rack density copper cannot reach, then CPO once it can be built at scale - early CPO adoption expected, but a completely different manufacturing technology whose yields will be very challenging early on. Arista builds CPO or NPO switches when customers ask; XPO timing is partly aligned with scale-up form factor and bandwidth density needs.
quarterly_data.figure: XPO early deployments second half of next year, really ramping in 2028, and probably 12 months behind that

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-UP IS ZERO TODAY: Breithaupt said there is 'zero in our guidance and zero revenue for Arista for scale up in 2026', with trials and pilots expected later next year once the Ethernet ecosystem comes together, and '2028 is when we get the revenue there'. Framework: scale-up splits into proprietary (NVLink and UALink), a commodity white-box play for lower value-add needs, and value-add Ethernet where Arista plays - with the open question being how much of the TAM Ethernet starts at and whether proprietary migrates to Ethernet as InfiniBand did. Lamoreaux argued the feature set is smaller in scale-up but reliability, security and telemetry still decide it.
quarterly_data.figure: zero in our guidance and zero revenue for Arista for scale up in 2026; 2028 is when we get the revenue there

quarterly_data.signal: TAM REVISION COMING: Breithaupt said the $105 billion TAM given at the October 2025 Analyst Day is being revisited for scale-up and scale-across because a lot has changed in under a year, with a revised TAM to be presented 'later this year'. She expects it to expand.
quarterly_data.figure: $105 billion TAM; October 2025; later this year

quarterly_data.signal: A NEW SCALE-ACROSS DRIVER - POWER POLICY, NOT JUST POWER SCARCITY: Lamoreaux said regulatory regimes and top-down government initiatives are becoming a distinct scale-across driver, citing South Korea, where policy is pushing distributed generation and local consumption of power. The consequence is that data center capacity federates around the country instead of concentrating, each site is capped by locally available power, and those clusters must be interconnected - which he said can shift the scale-across TAM quite a lot.
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure

quarterly_data.signal: ENTERPRISE / CAMPUS / INTERNATIONAL SHARE-GAIN DETAIL: Breithaupt put Arista at about 20%, 22% market share in data center and 5% in campus, campus going from USD 800 million in 2025 to USD 1.25 billion in 2026 - above market growth, so a share-gain story - with campus-first wins and VeloCloud SD-WAN now a full year in. Enterprises are pulling refreshes forward for security reasons (she claimed the lowest CVEs in the industry by a magnitude of 30x to 1, one EOS to patch instead of 50 to 60 to 70 people maintaining many operating systems). EMEA grew 36% last quarter; two 10% customers today with a third and potentially a fourth anticipated.
quarterly_data.figure: 20%, 22% market share in data center; 5% market share; USD 800 million in 2025 to USD 1.25 billion in 2026; EMEA last quarter had 36% growth; 30x to 1

quarterly_data.signal: SCALE-ACROSS PORT MECHANICS (mix itself matches the Q2 call's ~30% of the AI target): VP of Product Line Management Brendan Gibbs said data-center-interconnect scale-across is now 'a third of our business as part of the most recent guide' - the spine becomes geographically dispersed, so customers both re-use high-radix ports with ZR/ZR+ coherent DWDM pluggables AND deploy new platforms. Arista frames scale-across as a win only available to vendors that first won the back-end scale-out cluster.
quarterly_data.figure: scale across now a third of our business

quarterly_data.signal: SUPPLY / DEMAND QUALITY: CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said there is no pull-forward in the order book despite the shortage narrative - 'We don't see pull forward at all... it's 52-week lead time, so I don't think customers are going to lean in to 52 weeks unless they're pretty certain that it's something'. Supply is still not unconstrained going into next year (described as whack-a-mole), and she said that with a bit more supply Arista could beat even the raised FY2026 guide.

quarterly_data.quarter: Cisco Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-08-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel disclosed the next Silicon One scale-out chip: the G300, which has close to a quarter trillion transistors on 100-millimeter package substrate. Cisco operates in both scale-out systems (the G300) and scale-across systems (the P-Series chips), and sells hyperscalers full systems rather than chips alone. He framed scale-across as the answer to power limits - data centers are starting to get to be hundreds of kilometers apart but need to operate like one logical unit, which requires different chip design including debuffering so packet loss does not force a training run to restart.
quarterly_data.figure: Silicon One G300: close to a quarter trillion transistors on 100-millimeter package substrate

quarterly_data.quarter: Cisco Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-08-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: Silicon roadmap commitment: 'By 2029, we will be completely independent of merchant silicon providers because we will have made our own silicon.' Cisco makes its own silicon and its own photonics, and management says it would not have a hyperscaler business without that because hyperscalers want choice and diversity from the others in the market. Being in the silicon business is a five-year planning cycle versus 24 to 30 months for hardware, and Cisco expects to keep expanding into different use cases of silicon and to keep doing the same thing on the photonic side. Scale in Silicon One comes from over 960,000 customers to amortize silicon cost across volume segments.
quarterly_data.figure: completely independent of merchant silicon providers by 2029; over 960,000 customers

quarterly_data.quarter: Cisco Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-08-2026)
quarterly_data.signal: CFO Mark Patterson sized the installed-base refresh behind the non-AI demand floor: from equipment coming end of life and end of support in just the next few years, Cisco has identified over $100 billion worth of opportunity just for Cisco upgrade and refresh, and is also going after competitors' end-of-life installed base. Market share reports show Cisco not only holding share but taking back share in most, if not all, of the networking categories. Networking has now been double-digit growth for eight quarters in a row. Jeetu Patel added that campus and branch networking, historically pegged at the rate of GDP of 3%, 4%, has now been growing at 20% for several quarters.
quarterly_data.figure: over $100 billion worth of opportunity for Cisco upgrade and refresh; networking double-digit growth for eight quarters in a row; campus and branch growing at 20% for several quarters versus GDP of 3%, 4%

quarterly_data.signal: Record Q2 FY2026 revenue, above the high end of guidance (CFO Mark Patterson): total revenue $15.3 billion, up 10% year-over-year; product revenue $11.6 billion, up 14%; services revenue $3.7 billion, down 1%. Networking was the standout with growth of 21%, driven by AI infrastructure and campus refresh (double-digit growth in campus switching, data center switching, wireless, service provider routing, enterprise routing and compute); security down 4% (prior-generation declines and the Splunk shift to cloud subscriptions); collaboration up 6%. Non-GAAP EPS $1.04, up 11%; non-GAAP gross margin 67.5%, down 120 basis points, with product gross margin 66.4%, down 130 basis points, primarily on mix and higher memory costs; non-GAAP operating margin 34.6%, the highest in 4 quarters. Total RPO $43.4 billion, up 5%; product RPO up 8%, of which the long-term portion was $11.8 billion, up 11%.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $15.3 billion (up 10%); product revenue $11.6 billion (up 14%); Networking growth of 21%; non-GAAP EPS $1.04 (up 11%); non-GAAP gross margin 67.5%

quarterly_data.signal: Hyperscaler AI orders accelerating (CEO Chuck Robbins): AI infrastructure orders taken from hyperscalers totaled $2.1 billion in Q2, compared to $1.3 billion the prior quarter, and equal to the total orders taken in all of fiscal year '25, across silicon, systems and optics. Given strong demand for Silicon One systems and optics, Cisco raised its FY2026 expectation to AI orders in excess of $5 billion and over $3 billion of AI infrastructure revenue recognized from hyperscalers. Asked about the Silicon One vs optics mix in the bookings, Robbins said: 'We talked about this past quarter, the mix was 60% systems, 40% optics. And I think that's been reasonably consistent over the last few quarters.' The $5 billion does NOT include the recently announced P200 products, the G300, or the two optics products announced at Cisco Live. Orders are lumpy and nonlinear - 'less than a handful of these major customers' place them. In Q2 Cisco won 3 new use cases across these major players: 1 in optics and 2 on the systems side. CFO: 'You're seeing orders converting to revenue. I think that you're seeing a continued ramp as we move through the year', and he agreed with an analyst that this gives better visibility on revenue recognition into fiscal '27.
quarterly_data.figure: hyperscaler AI orders $2.1 billion in Q2 (vs $1.3 billion prior quarter); FY26 AI orders in excess of $5 billion; over $3 billion AI infrastructure revenue; mix 60% systems, 40% optics

quarterly_data.signal: Silicon One and optics launches: Cisco shipped its 1 millionth Silicon One chip in Q2 and plans to deploy the Silicon One architecture across its high-performance networking systems by fiscal year '29. At Cisco Live Amsterdam it introduced the 102.4 terabit per second G300 chip ('an exclusive group of silicon providers delivering over 100 terabits per second switching speeds') and launched 4 new systems powered by G300 - Cisco 8000 and Nexus 9000 102.4 terabit systems with air-cooled options for traditional data centers and a liquid cooled option for ground-up facilities. It also announced 2 new pluggable optics, a 1.6 terabit per second OSFP and an 800-gig LPO, both built with Cisco silicon photonics technology. Management cited programmability and power efficiency as the system/silicon differentiators, and customers' desire for silicon diversity as the starting point of hyperscaler interest.
quarterly_data.figure: 1 millionth Silicon One chip shipped; 102.4 terabit per second G300 chip; 4 new systems powered by G300; 1.6 terabit per second OSFP and 800-gig LPO

quarterly_data.signal: Acacia reported its strongest quarter to date with triple-digit growth in bookings. All major hyperscalers are deploying its coherent pluggable optics for data center interconnect and scale across use cases, with growth in both 400-gig and 800-gig coherent optics and transponder shipments and 800-gig pluggables 'ramping significantly'. Chuck Robbins called the optics portfolio '#1 in the world' and said 'we need to increase capacity to actually continue to deal with more and more demand there.'
quarterly_data.figure: strongest quarter to date; triple-digit growth in bookings; 800-gig pluggables ramping significantly

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity-constrained AI networking: asked about 51.2 terabit and 100 terabit data center switch order rates, Chuck Robbins said 'On the $5 billion and the 51.2 product, I think we're selling as much as we can build at this point. We see demand across a couple of major customers that are literally asking for as much as they can get. And we're seeing huge acceleration in the 800-gig optics. We're seeing huge acceleration, obviously, in the Acacia portfolio. So I think the demand is there, and we just need to continue to build capacity.' CFO added there were additional hyperscaler design wins in the quarter.
quarterly_data.figure: selling as much as we can build (51.2 product)

quarterly_data.signal: Memory cost response: Chuck Robbins addressed 'the recent significant increases in memory prices across the market' with 3 strategies - price increases already announced (with further adjustments as necessary), revising contractual terms with channel partners and customers to address evolving component prices, and using operating scale to negotiate favorable terms and secure supply. CFO Mark Patterson said advanced purchase commitments are up $1.8 billion in just the last 90 days and up about 73% year-over-year, 'A big chunk of that is around memory'; the Q3 gross margin guide reflects mix and memory prices, and some of the memory impact 'is just timing' and should improve as pricing and Ts and Cs changes run through. No significant pull-forwards seen (pipeline building in out quarters); customers understand the increases as industry-wide and are not deferring strategic investments. Core networking carries less memory content than compute platforms, so the increases are 'more nominal', and UCS is not as big a share of Cisco as it is for peers.
quarterly_data.figure: advanced purchase commitments up $1.8 billion in the last 90 days, up about 73% year-over-year

quarterly_data.signal: Guidance (assumes current tariffs and exemptions remain in place through fiscal 2026): Q3 FY2026 revenue $15.4 billion to $15.6 billion, non-GAAP gross margin 65.5% to 66.5%, non-GAAP operating margin 33.5% to 34.5%, non-GAAP EPS $1.02 to $1.04, tax rate approximately 19%. Full fiscal year 2026 revenue $61.2 billion to $61.7 billion and non-GAAP EPS $4.13 to $4.17 - positioned for Cisco's strongest year ever. Management said the Q3 gross margin step-down is driven by mix (hardware ramping faster than prior launches) and memory prices.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 revenue $15.4 billion to $15.6 billion; Q3 non-GAAP gross margin 65.5% to 66.5%; FY26 revenue $61.2 billion to $61.7 billion; FY26 non-GAAP EPS $4.13 to $4.17

quarterly_data.signal: Order breadth: total product orders grew 18% year-over-year (10% excluding hyperscalers). Service provider and cloud orders grew 65%, driven by triple-digit order growth across hyperscalers; telco and cable orders up almost 20% combined; public sector up 11%; enterprise up 8%. By geography, Americas up 23%, EMEA up 11%, APJC up 15%. Networking product orders grew more than 20%, a sixth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth (service provider routing, data center switching, campus switching, wireless, servers, industrial IoT). Data center switching has grown double digits in 6 of the last 8 quarters; industrial IoT double digits for 7 consecutive quarters; Wi-Fi 7 up 80% sequentially. The campus refresh - an installed base of 'tens of billions of dollars' nearing end of support - is at 'the top of the first inning' and a 'multiyear, multibillion-dollar opportunity'.
quarterly_data.figure: product orders up 18% (10% excluding hyperscalers); service provider and cloud orders up 65%; networking product orders more than 20%

quarterly_data.signal: AI beyond hyperscalers: Cisco took $350 million in AI orders from neocloud, sovereign and enterprise customers in Q2 and has a growing pipeline in excess of $2.5 billion for its high-performance AI infrastructure portfolio. In Q2 it announced plans to form a joint venture with AMD and HUMAIN to deliver up to 1 gigawatt of AI infrastructure by 2030; the JV expects to begin operations this calendar year, with 100 megawatts in Saudi Arabia as Phase 1. Sovereign is not expected to have a meaningful FY2026 impact ('purely upside'); neocloud ramp expected to begin in the second half but 'really be FY '27'.
quarterly_data.figure: $350 million AI orders in Q2 (neocloud, sovereign, enterprise); pipeline in excess of $2.5 billion; JV up to 1 gigawatt by 2030, 100 megawatts Phase 1

quarterly_data.signal: Transition stance on CPO and scale-up: on co-packaged optics Chuck Robbins said 'we absolutely believe it's going to happen. We don't believe it's actually imminent right now' - Cisco demonstrated the technology '2 years ago or more' and will build it as customers want it, but today customers want choice and the separation of optics and silicon to avoid lock-in; Cisco instead announced the 800-gig LPO for power savings in AI scale out. On scale-up: no announcements yet, but Cisco plans to participate and expects future scale-up products and revenue ('stay tuned').
quarterly_data.figure: no specific figure
